body.t: Moreover Job continued his Parable.
Why doth Job call what he had to say a Parable? The Origi¬
nal word signifies to rule, to govern, to govern as a Prince,
para-vhose righteous Precepts and Commands, whose Lawes and
Counsels, his people ought to obey: Speeches or Sentences which
are full of wisdom and of truth are called Parables for a threefold
Feason.
First, Because Parables and wise Sentences rule over the spirit:
of men, as Princes and Magistrates do over their bodies or out¬
ward man. Parables carry so convincing a light, so great an autho¬
ricy in them, that every mans Judgment and understanding sub¬
mits and falls down before them, such words bear rule and
sway. And though many contradict truth, & rebel against it, yet
truth will subdue, even them to its power, who would not submit
toits rule, nor bow to its Scepter. And Job might well call what
he had to say, a Parable, a collection of tuling sentences, seeing
the issue his friends, who were no friends to what he said, were
forced to yield themselves up to it, and submit to him by the final
sentence ot determination of God himself.
Secondly, Parables are so called, because such speeches came
usually from the mouths of Princes and greit Persons; they were
speeches of Rulers, therefore ruling speeches. Sotomon spake pro¬
verbs of Parables, who was a great King, and ruled over men
more by wisdome than he did by power.
Thirdl/, Because whether men will submit to such speeches
and truths or no, yet their Judgments, actions and opinions must
be tryed and ruled by them. Pambles are touchstones of truth,
they are rules, and therefore ought to rule.
Again, Others derive the O.iginal word which we rendet a Pa¬
rable, from a root uhich signifies to liken, or to make lihe; this also
suits well with the mture of Patables, which are usually expressed
by Similes or Similitudes, comparing one thing with another, or
pora-one thing to anothef (i Matb. 13.3.) At that time Jesus spake

bles in that Chapter; and what were those Parables? they were

rable, intimating all sorts of Gospel-Hearers, by four sorts of
ground. There also you have the Parable of the grain of Mustard¬

with a cole, they are accounted ( as Tob was) the vilest of the sons
of men, and yet ( though the Lord knows it is otherwise with
them)he lets it be so with them. He lets the dirt stick upon them,
even upon the face of their reputation, and uill not wash it off,
They whom God hath made cleane, the world either makes or
reputes uncleane. As that which is highly esteemed among men
an abomination in the sight of God, so they who are high¬
esteemed of God, are an abomination in the sight of men.
These sufferings of the Saints in their owne credit, ot in the opi¬
nion of men, serve the holy ends and purposes of God, as much
any of their sufferings, whether in body or state, by the oppressions
and persecutions of men. And therefore Saints are detained under
these tryalls as well as any other, till those holy ends are served;
and longer than that, they shall not be detained under them. This
tongue-rod either of wicked men, or of mistaken and misunder¬
standing brethren, shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous;

0029.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bock of JOR. Verf. 2.

body.t: Though God take away their Judgment for the present, yet at
last he will give judgment for them. David was not onely risen
up to that assurance, but had it in experience (Psal. 9.3,4,5.)
when mine enemies are turned bach, they shall fall and perish at
thy presence; for thou hast maintained my right, and my cause, thou
sattest in the throne judging right, or in righteousnesse. David found
God standing up presently for him, and asserting his innocency,
he found God sitting in his throne, and giving right judgment
against his enemy. But is not God alwayes upon his thronc ?or doth
he any thing at any time upon his throne but what is right ? Woe
tothose who thinke otherwise; God is alwayes upon his throne,
and can doe nothing but right there. But he doth not alwayes give
out, or declare his righteous judgments, or the righteousnesse of
his judgments; All men have not the fruit or benefit of them, as
David then had. Thou hast rebuked the heathen, thou hast destroyed
the wiched, thou hast put out their name for ever and ever. Thus the
Lord did execute Judement sor David even upon the place.
He gives a like report of the present appearance of God for him
Pial. 41. 12.) As for me thou upholdest me in mine integritie;
that is, while I walk uprightly, sincerely, and with a single heart
thou takest my part, and maintainest me against all mine enemies,
or not withstanding the opposition of mine enemies, thou doest
maintaine in me a desite and purpose to walke still sincerely, up¬
rightly, and in the singleness of my heart. And indeed we have
great reason to hold fast, and to hold on in our integrity, while the
Lord undertake’s to uphold us in our integrity. And if he should
let us fall in our integrity, or our integrity fall for a while, yet we
have a promise (Psal. 27. 6.) that the Lord will doe it for all his
people at last, or in the fittest season. Waite upon the Lord, trust
also in him, and he shall bring it to passe; he shall bring forth thy
righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noone day. Though
thy judement or right be like midnight, darke, and obscure, so
that none can see it; though the Lord himselfe (as Tob here
speakes ) seemeth to have taken away thy Judgment, yet taïte
while, and thou shalt see a glo ious turne, thou thalt see darkness
turned to light, and midnight to noone day; thou shalt see God
bringing forth thy righteousnesse as the licht, and bringing backon
restoring thy jud gment (which he tooke away ) like unte the noone¬
day. Thus Paul comforted himselse when God had taken away

0030.head: Chap.27. An Exposition npon the Book of JOB. Vers.2.

body.t: his judgment, and he lay under the severest judgment of men,
(1. Cor . 3.4,5, 6. ) Mith me it is a very small thing that I should
be Tudges of yoa, or of mans Judgment (I know men censure me li¬
beraliy) for I bnow nothing by my selfe (I am cleare in my oune
conscience) yet I'am net heareby Jastified, But he that Judgeth
me is the Lord. God judgeth all men presently, as tonis owne
knoulecg of their estate, and he will ere long publish the know¬
ledge ot their state to others, even in the eares and tothe open
viewsof all. Therefore (the Apostle concludes, v. 5. ) Judg no¬
thing before the time untill the Lord come, mho both will bring to
light the hidden things of darbness, and will manisest the counsels of
the heart: and then shall ever y man (who hath been falsely accused
apd wrongsully difgraced by men) have praise of God. In the
Great Judgment God will take away that Judgment of out ward
apprebation from all wicked men which the world had given
them, & he will give that Judgment of outward approbation to all
godly men, which himselfe had taken away from them while the
were in this world;and they shall say in that day, The Lord liveth
who hath restored our Judgment, which he, vas pleased (as Job
saitn here ) once to take away.
And the almighty mho hath ve xed my soule.
Here againe we are to repeate or suppose the oath, As Ged li-
veth, nho hath taken auay my judgment, and ( as) the Almight
(liveth) who hath vexed my soul. This title of God almighty,
notes, first, the strength; secondly, the goodnesse of God. As the
Lerd is powerfull, so he is the spring, and fountaine of goodnesse
and mercy to his people; neverthelels though the Lord be thus al¬
might y, though he be thus mercifull, and good in himfelf, yet (saith
Toh) he vexeth my soul. The text is, He mabeth my soule bitter,
He is bitter to me; it is usual to expresse affliction by bitternesse,
and the inflicting of affliction upon any, by imbittering them,
There is a threefold notion of bitternesie in Scripture; First, Sin
called bitternesse ( Hos. 12.14.) Ephraim provoked him to anger
most bitterty. We translate in the superlative; the text is, Ephraim
provoked him to anger with bitternesses. What provokes God to
anger? it is sin; and what is sin? bitternesse, yea bitternesses;there
is a collection of all bitternesses in any sin, how many bitternes¬
ses are there then in a collection of many sins! Ephraim provoted

0031.head: Chap.27. An Exp-fition upon the Book of JOB. Veri, 2.

body.t: him to anger with bitternesses, that is, with many sins. We render
well, Ephraim provoked him to anger most bitterly; either imply¬
ing the degree of Ephraims sinfulness, which provoked God to
anger, his was a high provocation, or implying the degree of that
anger which the Lord expressed by reason of that provocation;
The Lord was most bitterly angry at the sinfull provocations of
Ephraim. And this complyes with the following notion of Bitter¬
ness in Scripture.
Secondly, Anger, and wrath it selfe is called bitternesse, or
bitter thing; anger is hot, and heate makes the naturall humour
bitter; whence by allusion anger is expressed by bitternesse, be¬
cause it doth imbitter the spirit, as much heite imbittereth the
stomicke. The word is used in that prophesie of the Ram, and the
He-goat (Din. 8.8.) And I saw him (that is, the He-goite) come
close to the Ram, and he was moved mith choller against him; so we
tranflate; the text is (’tis the word here ufed in Job) he was im¬
bittered against him, or vexel at him. The Goite (or Alexander
King of Gretce) was imbittered against the Ram (or against Da¬
rius the King of Persia) and smote the Ram, and brake his two
hornes. Solomon saith (Pro. 17.11.) An evill man setketh only
rebellion; some read it, He sechet b onely anger; The text is, An
evil man secketh onely bitternesse, chat is, to imbitter the spirits of
others; he careth not how much anger he kindles among men,
and therefore he loves to blow the coiles. Whereas it is the bu¬
siness of a gracious man to sweeten, and quiet the spirits ef others.
He is peaceable himselse to others, and a peace-maker between
others; But an evil man seeketh onely anger.
Thirdly, Bitternesse is put for affliction. That which makes
our lives bitter tous, may well be called bitterness. When that
good woman Naomi came home, afflicted, and emptied, to
her freinds and fellow Citizens, who had formerly knowne her,
they being much moved between compassion and wonder at her
sad condition, said, is this Naomi! Is it possible; What is this
Naomi! Then she said unto them ( Ruth. 1. 20 ) Call me not
Naomi ( that is, beautifull) but call me Marab, ( that is, bitter
for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me; I went out full,
and the Lord hath brought me home emptie. And as bitterness is put
for worldly sorrow, or for that sorrow which ariseth from trou¬
bles or wants in the things of the world: so also for Spirituall or

0032.head: Chap.37. An Exposition npon the Bork of JOB. Vers.2.

body.t: Godly sorrow. (Lech. 12. 10.) They shall loob upon me mhom
they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mournethfor
bis only Son, aud they shall be in bitternesse for him, as one that is in
bitterness for his first-born. That which the Prophet calls mourn¬
ing in the former part of the verse,he calls being in bitterness in the
latter; As it is an evil and a bitter thing to sin against God, so
sinning against God should be followed with that good, but bitte:
thing, mourning or godly sorrow. Here Job was vexed or im¬
bittered, not so much withisorrow for his sins, as with the sence
of Gods afflicting hand in the tryal of his graces. Thus the Al¬
mighty (saith he) hath vexed my soul,
He did not say, the almight y had vexed his body er estate, though
the Lord did vex both, or him in both; He pitched only upon
the vexation of his soul; His affliction went deep, it reached not
oply his skin and flesh, but his soul and spirit; yet when he saith,
The Almighty hath vexed my soul, he doth not meane it of
soul-affliction, either alone, or in opposition to the afflictions of
the body, such as are trouble of mind for sin, disquietness of con¬
science, and sence of divine wrath, but he means thus much ouly
(Isuppose) in this place, That his troubles were greatand but¬
densome, so great and burdensome, that he was smitten all over,
and felt the sad effects of the Lords afflicting hand in the grief of
his soule, as well as in the pains of his body. The Almighty hath
vexed my soul.
Observe;
First, The Lord hath all pomer in his hand.
He were not Almighty, if he had not. Some men have presumed
themselves able to do all things, and so have most blasphemoufty
usurped this attribute of almightinesse, but none ever were so.
Secondly, Observe;
It is not for want of power that God doth not pres ently relieve
and help his distressed servants.
As God never wants strength to afflict, so not to deliver. He is
alwayes furnished with power to execute whatsoever he hath
will to appoynt. When we lye in affliction unrelieved, we are
more ready to question the power of God, than our own sinful¬
ness. The Jewes had such apprehensions ef God, as we may colræet
E

0033.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOR. Vers.2.

body.t: from that redargution in the prophet (Isa. 59.1.) The Lords
hand is not shortned that it cannot save; As if he had said, ye thinke
ye are in a distresse so deepe that the Lords hand is not long e¬
nough now ( though it have been heretofore) to reach your sal¬
vation, whereas in truth the Lords hand is not shortned that
cannot save: The reason why ye are not delivered, is not because
God hath not power to deliver you, but because your sins stand
in the way of your deliverance. Tour iniquities have separated be¬
toeen yon and yourGod, and your sins have hid his face from you that
he will not heare. Till our sins be removed either by pardon or re¬
pentance, or both, troubles will not remove from us. While the
fountaine of goodis separated from us, evill must needs abide with
us. Our helpe is alwayes in the hand of God, but he hath not al¬
wayes awill to helpe us, and the most usual reason why his will
not to save or deliver us from or out of trouble, is because our
will is so big with sin, and so much in the deliverance ot it,
Thirdly, observe;
The Lord is sometimes so farr from putting forth his power
releive his precious oues, that he puts it forth to afflict ana
lay them low.
To comfort the soulis the most proper worke ot God, and yet
'tis his work also to vex the soule. And as he speaks to the wicked
in his wrath and vexeth them in his sore displeasure (Psal.2.5.)
so tis his pleasure (yet not without infinite wisdom and gracious
intendments also) to speak to many who are Godly in his anger,
and to vexe their soules under the severest dispensations.
Fourthly, Observe;
Afflictions are to the soule as bitter things to the tast.
No chastning for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous,
(Heb. 12.11.) Though affliction bring forth peaceable fruits of
righteousnesse to them that are exercised thereby, yet to be under
that exercise is sorrow and trouble; Even those chastnings which
are (as to the issue) onely for the tryall and cleansing of the soul,
are also (in the way) a vexation totne soul.
Fisthly, Observe;
Sairts acknowledge the hand of God in all their afflictions,
The almighty hath vexed my soule, saith Tob. He had many o¬

0034.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bak of JOR. Vers.2.

body.t: ther hands upon him, but he tooke most notice of the hand of
God, as hath been shewed at the 21. verse of the first Chapter,
and else-where in this Book. Faith seeth him who is invisible,
vexing as well as comforting; And ’tis comfort to Saints, not only
to remember God in their afflictions, but to remember that it
God who afflicts them.
Sixthly Note;
A godly man hath good thoughts of God, while he ascribes his pe¬
nall evills or sufferings unto God.
Tob knew and acknowledged that God was not onely good in
himselfe, but good to him while he vexed his soul; while God af¬
flicts us and makes us poore, or sick, while he strips us naked of
riches, children, friends and relations, yet we should say (as Da¬
vid, (Plal. 73.1.) Traly God is good to Israel, even to all them
that are upright in heart. While the Lord vexeth our souls, our
soules should magnifie the Lord. While the Lord makes our souls
bitter, our souls should sweeten the dealings of God. While the
Lord troubles us we should not be displeased, yea we should be
well-pleased with the Lord. God doth his people no hurt, much
lesse doth he intend them hurt when he makes them smart; There¬
fore it is their dutie, even when they smart, to make the fairest re¬
ports of him to all that come about them. God is such a fountaine
as sends forth both bitter waters & sweet, as to our present sence,
but all the waters which he sends forth are sweete as to our future
benefit; therefore though sense say of some of them they are bit¬
ter, yet let faith say of all of them they are sweet.
Seventhly, Observe;
Saints afflictions are osten very deepe afflictions.
They goe downe to the very soul. Not only were Tosephs feete
hurt in the stocks, but the iron entred into his soule, as the old tran¬
slation hath it (Psal. 105.18.) or, as we put in the Margin, his
soule came into iron ; that is, he was afflicted, or (as Tob here
speaks) vexed to his soule. As the uord of God (Heb. 4. 2.)
pierceth to the dividing, so the rod of God can peirce to the grie¬
ving and paining of soule and spirit, of the joynts and marrow.
Thus Tob deciphers God in his dealing uith him; As Gol liveth,
mho hath taken away my Judgment, and the almighty who hath vex¬

0035.head: Chap.27. An Exposition apon the Bock of J0R. Vers.3.

body.t: ed my soule; But what was Tobs oath or whether did it tend? the
two next verses shew us, First, the continuance of this oath upon
nim: secondly, the concernment of it, or about what he tooke this
solemne oath. The former we have in the third verse, the latter
in the fourth.
Vers. 3. All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God
is in my nostrills, (v.4.) My lips shall not speahe mic¬
Lednesse, nor my tongue utter deceit.
Job takes his oath, not for a dayor a yeare, but for his life, als
the mhile my breath is in me, that is, as long as I live. While breath
continues, life continues. It is said (Gen, 2. 7.) The Lord brea¬
thed into man the breath ot life, The hebrew word for breath hath
an affinity with that by which the heavens are expressed in the
same language; implying (say some) that the breath of man came
from heaven, or was of God; The breath of man was not created
with man in the forming of the body, as it was with the beasts;
but after the body was formed God infused the breath, and there¬
fore Moses in that text fpeakes distinctly concerning man; First,
The Lord God formed man out of the dust of the carth, & (then) brea¬
thed into his nostrills the breath of life, and man became a living
soule. So then, To have breath in us, is to have life in us, or it is
circumlocution of life, and as soone as breath departs life departs,
we dye. It is said (1 Kings 17. 17.) That the Son of the Wo¬
man, the Mistresse of the house, fell sick, and his sicknesse was so
sore that there was no breath left in him, that is, he dyed. When Eu¬
tychus falling from the third loft was taben up dead, Paul went
downe and fell on him, and imbracing him said, trouble not your
selves for his life is in him. The Grecke is, His soule is in him.
They who tooke him up concluded him dead, because he did not
breath, knowing that when breath goes, life goes too; But Paul
fercht him againe by prayer, and his breath returned. Wheu Paul
embraced him, breath re-entred him; And therefore he saith be¬
remptorily his life is in him, either because it was theo returned,
or because he knew it would; according o the usual language of
faith he spa ke of it, as of a thing already none. Sence and reason
said, he was dead, because his breath was gone; but faith said his
life was in him, knowing that God was able to bring the breath
back againe. Mans life amounts only to this, He hath his breath

0036.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bork of JOR. Vers.3.

body.t: his nostrils. (Ila. 2. 22.) Or (as Tob speakes )breath is in him,
All the while my breath is in me,
And the spirit of God in my nostrils.
This latter clause is of the same signification with the former,
and is but a repetition in other words,yet there is som difference
of opinion, what should be here meant by the Spirit of God,
There are among the ancients who understand, the holy Spirit,
not only the Spirit ot God, but God the Spirit. And they tell us,
That we have a description or specification of the whole Trinity in
this Text; By the living God, understanding the Father, and by the
almighty, the Sonne, and by the Spirit of God, the Holy Ghost. But
cannot comply with this interpretation; For though I doubt not
but Tob had the Spirit of God, yet here he is describing his nitu¬
rall life, not his spiritua!; And it is plaine that he intends nothing
but his niturall life by the Spirit of God, because he calleth it the
Spirit of God in his nostrils. The holy sanctifying, comforting Spi¬
rit, is not said to be a Spirit in our nostrils; that’s no way suitable
to Scripture-speaking, which saith, That the Holy Spirit of God
dwels in our hearts, or in out inner man, as also in our bodyes, but
never in our nostrils. So then Spirit is the same with breath. As
for that addition, The Spirit of God, it signifieth only thus nuch,
that God is the maker or author of the Spirit here spoken of, not
that the Spirit here spoken of is God our maker;or that God is the
efficient cause of this Spirit, as of all other creatures, not that this
Spirit is God by nature. So that when Tob saith, Al the mhile my
breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, his scope is,
to give utmost assurance to his friends, that he intended to hold his
owne to the utmost. His breath he granted might quickly passe
away, and the Spirit in his nostrils sit upon his lips ready to take
leave and be gone; but if his life should continue long, and he
anpeare rather like a Home-dweller than a stranger or sojourner
incois worid, yet he was fully purposed to abide and continue in
the ne opinion and defence of himselfe unto the end.
Hence Obt rve;
Pirst, Life is ef God.
pirir wvnereby we live the life of nature, as well as the Spi¬
suhe eby de live the life of Grace, the Spirit in our nostijls as
An Expofition upon the Book of
OB.
Chap.27.
well as the Spirit in our hearts is the gift, the onely gift of God;
allthe powers in heaven and earth ( without God) cannot give
breath, nor make life. Art hath imitated living things, but never
was there any artist which could make taings live; the Painter can
make the image of a man, but he cannot put lile into his image,
God onely doth that.
First, Then our life depends upon God, we live or dye at his
pleasure. ( Psal. 104. 29.) Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled;
thou tak est away their breath, they dye and returne to their dust.
Life is breath given, death is breath taken away. Dantel tells Ne¬
buchadnezzar, TheGod in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all
thy wayes, hast thou not honoured (Chap. 5. 23.) He describeth
God in his Greatnesse by having that Great Kings breath in his
hand, that is, in his pouer; He gave it thee, and he can take
from thee when he will. David puts this power among those Ex¬
cellencies of God for which he is to be magnified by mankinde
(Psal. 66. S, 9.) O blesse our God, ye people, and make the voyce
his praise to be heard, mhich holdeth our soule in life. The Hebrew
(as our Margin hath it ) is, which putteth our soul in life. We may
take in both readings, and not at all enlarge the text beyond its
due bounds, for God first putteth our soule in life, that is, he cau¬
seth’our soule, that is, our selves or our persons to live by bringing
and uniting soule and body together. Secondiy, He holdeth our
soule in life, by preserving or delivering us from those daily dan¬
gers and evils which threaten to separate or divorce our soules
from our bodyes. If God did not hold and keepe our soules in
life, our soules could not continue in life one minute. No sooner
doth the living God withdraw his hand of preservation, but man
is among the dead, or upon the borders of dissolution; diseases
and dangers would soone breake this union, and unty this marri¬
age-knot between soule and body, if God did not hold it : when
God lets goe his hold, out it goes, when God calleth, out it must.
As God said to Abraham ( Gen 12. 1.) Get thee out of thy Coun¬
try, and from thy bindred, and from thy fathers hause; God called
him from his owne home, and he willingly obeyed; So when God
calles our spirit out of the body, and commands it to dislodge,
must dislodge and come out whether we will or no. And secing
our life or breath depends upon God, and a call from him fetch¬
leth it forthat any time, let us pray (to speake in allusien to that

0038.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOB. Vers.3.

body.t: of Christ in the Gospel about the miseries that were to come up¬
on Terusalem, let us (I say ) pray ) that the flight of it may not be
the winter of sin, in the night of ignorance, or on the Saboath,
(I meane Satans Saboath) of carnal security and impenitency.
Seeing our breath must de part when God calls, it is our wisdome
make ready for our departure. It is best to be ready and pre¬
pared for that which we cannot avoid, how unready and un-pre¬
pared soever we are. Most live as if their life were in their owne
hand or at their own dispose, & not in the hand or dispose of God,
They who live as they list, seem to say, they can live as long as they
list. Let us remember, that as we are daily dying, and that as
cannot be many dayes before we must die, so we may die any day.
As it is appoynted for all men once to dye by a general decree,
soit is appoynted by a speciall decree when every man must dye.
This decree is in the breast of God, in whose hand our breath is,
Therefore as the Prophet exhorts (Zeph. 2. 1,2.) let us gather
our selves together, yea gather together (in the acting of faith
and every grace) before the decree bring forth, for our gathering
our fathers in the Grave,
Secondly, Observe;
Our life is but breath in our nostrills.
Such is the frailty of mans life, that his life stands alwayes atthe
doore, as if it were taking leave ot him. How soone may that be
gone, which cannot stay when our breath is gone? When the Holy
Ghost would shew how poore a thing man is, and how little or
rather how not at all to be trusted, or reckoned upon, He saith,
Cease ye from man, whose breath iu in his nostrills (Ifa. 2. 22.)As
if that were the most disparaging expression of mans life. Why
should we keepe so much adoe about any man living, seeing his
breath, and so his life, may be gone before he or we can doe any
thing. And as the Prophet calleth us off from relyance upon man
in generall, because his breath is in his nostrills; So the Psalmist
upon the same reason calleth us off from relyance upon great men
inspeciall, knowing how apt we are to rely upon them, and to
give the Gods of the earth that honour which is due onely to the
God of heaven, (Psal, 146.4, 5.) Put not jour trust in Priuces,
nor in the son of man, in mhom there is no helpe; his breath goetb
forth, he returnes to dust, in that very day his thoughts perish.

0039.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition apon the Book of J02. Vers.3

body.t: unlesse breath goe forth we dye, and death is nothing else but the
going forth of the breath. Life is the going forth of the breath
by respiration, and death is the going forth of the breath by ex¬
spiration. And how soone may respiring be changed into exspi¬
ring ? And as we dye when our breath goes out but returnes not,
when it cannot get out. The body hath been called the prison ot
the soul, and so in some sence it is;but here is a riddle, The keep¬
ing of the prisoner is quite contrary to that of other prisoners;
we keep prisoners by shutting up the doores, but if you shut up
the doores of your body, the mouth and nostrils, you loose your
prisoner, the soul gets presently out : Ilulesse the breath have li¬
bertie to passe out, you cannot hold it. The way to keepe the
breath in, is to give it free passage out; if the outward ayre be
kept out, and the breath kept in, life is lost, and we know how
fmall amatter will doe this; A gnat, a fly, the stone of a Raison,
single haire have done it in great examples. Therefore let us
cesse from other men, but chiefly from our selvs, seing we & they
are so soone ceasing: let us not over rate the persons of other men,
nor (which we are very apt to doe ) our own, for our breath is in
our Nostrills. Thus Job describes himselfe in his mortal state,
All the mhile my breath is in me, and the Spirit of God in my no¬
strils; As if he had said, This is the short and the long, the als
of my resolutions, while I am in this world, that whether my
life or stay in this world be long or short, I am strongly resolved,
That
Vers. 4. My lips shall not speake michednesse, nor my tongue utter
deceit.
In this verse fob removes two evils or diseases, or two evill dis¬
eases of the tongue from himselfe, Fiest, the speaking of miched¬
nesse, which is openly evill; Seconoiy, the speaking of deceit, which
closely evill. These tuo are joyned as in the text, so (Psa, 10.
7.) His ( that is, the wicked mans) mouth is full of cursiug deceit
and fraud : srom both these instruments and engines of the
wicked, David prayeth earnestly for deliverance (Psa. 120.2.
Deliver my soule, O Lord, from lying lips, and from a deceitfull
tongue. And here Job protests :gainst beth these tongue-abomi¬

greatest not ouly seriousness, but holiness.
And when we translate fob speaking thus, God forbid that
should justifie you; he prayes that God would keep it upon hi¬
heart for ever, not to doe or never to have any thing to do with
thing so repuguant both to his duty and conscience; as if he had
said, I should defile my felf, if I should ploase you, jea, I shoald con¬
demn my self, if I snould justifie you in this, and so betray my own
innocenc y to your angrounded censure and opinion of me. Some ex¬
pound Job yet higher, as implying himself worthy to be excom¬
municated and thrust out of the company of all that were godly
as a heathen and prophane person, in case he should render up
himself to their judgment of him, or justifie them in their con¬
demnatory sentence passed upon him. Thus highly he resents it,
and turneth from it with deepest indignation, God forbid, &c.
Hence Note;
A gracious heart doth not only deny to do evil, but hatb an ab¬
borrence against the doing of evill.
As corrupt nature is not only backuard and enilling to doe
good, but hath an enmity against it, so Grace doth not only stay
us from, but stirreth up an holy enmity against every uncleane
thing. The spirit of a godly man riseth, and his stomack turneth
at the sight of sin. As they who are most emptyed of sin by Go¬
spel-repentance, complain most that they are full of it. And as
they who have least sin in them, are most burdened with the sin
that remains in them, so likewise, they most abominate both the
committing of any sin, and every sin committed, whether by them¬
selves or others. The Apostle reckons this among the effects ot
true repentance (2 Cor. 7.11.) In that ye sorrowed after a golly
sort, bebold mhat cartfulness is wrought in jou, nhat clearing of jour

0052.head: Chap.27. An Expositon npon the Boct of J.OR.

body.t: Vert-
selues, qua what indignation; that is, indignation against your
selves, even for faylings and wezknesses, much more for any thing
done by you, or among you, which may be called wickedness, ora
provocation. Thus David chargeth folly upon his own soul,
(Psal. 73.22.) So foolish was I and ignorant, I was as a beast bi¬
fore thee. When he reflected upon his finful envy at the prospe¬
rity of the wicked, he rebuked himself, as a fool, as a beast, as
an ignoramus, as one that knew nothing of the providential dis¬
peusations of God. And thus Job ( being convinced of his over¬
boldness with God, upon the clear discoveries ot his holiness and
soveraignty) abhorred himself, repenting in dust and ashes (Chap.
42.6.) He that abhorrs himself for what he hath done, cannot
but abhorre what he hath done, as much as he abhorreth himself
for doing it. As a godly man repenting abhorreth the evil
which ( being overpowered by a temptation) he hath done; so,
when he is in a composed frame, he abhorreth to do that evil
which he is tempted. David saith (Psal. 119. 104.) Ihate e¬
very false may; I hate not only the way, when I have been misled
into it, but I hate to go in it; and he professeth at the 163.verse
of that Psalme, I hate and abhor lying, but tby lax do I love.
To abstain from and forbear lying, is a signe of a gracious heart,
much more to hate and abhor it. A godly man not only doth
that which is good,but he delights to do it, his soul cleaves to it;
he is in his element when he is doing it, nothing comes more sui¬
tably to him, than the business of his duty, he loveth to do it,
yes he loveth it when he cannot do it (Rom. 7. 22.) Paul com¬
plained much that his corruptions clogged, hindered, and shackled
him, he was in lime-twigs, as to the doing of good, yet ( saith
he) I delight in the Law of God after the inmard man; that is, the
inward man delightfully moves after the law of God, when Fam
basely moved by my corrupt heart, and stirred by temptation a¬
gainst it. Now (I say) as a godly man not only chooseth to doe
the holy will of God, but delights and rejoyceth to do it, and
hath sweet content in doingit; so likewise a godly man not only
resuseth to do the will of the flesh, or to follow the course of the
world, but hates to do it, and is never so discontented with him¬
self,as when through carelesnefs and neglect of bis watch he hath
been overtaken and done it. A carnal man may forbear the do¬
ing of evil, and do what is materially good, but he never ab¬

0053.head: An Expofition upon the Bock of JOB. Vers. 5.

body.t: Chap.27.
horres what is evill, nor delights in whit is good. Though he ab¬
staine from acting those things, which God forbids; yet he doth
not say (with Job) Gol forbid, I sbould act them. David gives thàt
as one of the most distinguishing characters of a wicked man,
(Plal. 36.4.) He deviseth mischeife upon his bed, he setteth him¬
selfe in a way that is not good; he abhorreth not evill. And though
he doth good, yet his heart doth not cleave to nor delight in it.
To delight in good, is better than the doing of it, and to abhorre
evil, is better than abstaining from it. And if we compare the na¬
ture of sin, with the new nature of a godly man, we may see cleare
grounds, why his abstinence from sin, is joyned with the abhor¬
tence of it.
First, Sin is filthy and uncleane in its nature, the Scripture calls
vomit; we loath and abhor what is filthy and uncleane, espe¬
cially our vomit. And to shew how much sin is to be abominated,
is called abominable, yea an abomination (Pro. 12. 22.)And that
wicked Idolatrous people, the heathen Romans, who were skil¬
full to destroy ( and aftet their laying desolite many other lands,
at last, layd the holy Land desolate, to punish the unholinesse of
them that dwelt in it, they I say)are called the Abomination of de¬
solation ( Math. 24.15.) no mat vaile if those persons and actions
are abhorred by others, which are themselves abominable; it
marvailous that they are not more abhorred by all those, who
through grace) are made sensible of their abomination. When
the river was turned to blood, and stunke, the Egyptians loathed
to drink ofthe water ot the river, (Exod. 7. 14.) As corrupt
water, so corrupt actions stinke in the nostrils of a godly man,
how much more in the nostrils of God; there is a samenesse of
spirit (in God and in a godly man) in reference to the thing
selfe, though infinitely different in degree;sin stinks in the nost ills
of agodly min, as well as in the nostrills of God, and therefore
he loaths to drinke it, and cannot beare it when he hath, but must
vomit it up againe.
Secondly, Sin and all sinfull wayes are presented to a godly
man, as extreamly hurtful, poysonous, and deadly; Nature, much
more grace, turneth away from those things that are destructive.
Shall I meddle with that which will be my death? (saith a Godly
man) shall I suck the blood of a toade, or eate the flesh ot a ser¬
pent? shall I doe this? The Lord said to Moses (Exod. 4.2, 3.)

0054.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verf.5.

body.t: What is that in thy band? and he said a rod, and he said, cast it on
the ground, and he cast it on the ground, and it became a serpent, aud
Moses fled from it; there is an antipathy in the nature of a man
against hurtfull creatures. A man before conversion hath sin in
his hand, and heart too; but when once converted, he throweth
his sin out of his hand, as Moses did his rod, and then he seeth it
serpent, a hurtfull noxious thing, and then he fleeth from it.
That sin which an unregenerate man carrieth as a pleasant rod in
his hand, he finds to be a stinging serpent when he is regenerate.
The heart being changed, our opinion quickly changeth concern¬
ing those wayes and practices, which before were most pleasing
us; And as Cod hath in his commandements forbidden us to
doe evill, so we (with holy Job in the text) say God forbid, that
we should doe it. But it may be questioned, what there was in
this action so sinfull, that his spirit rose up so against it, or that he
should say, God forbid I fhould doe it.
See wbat it wis.
Gol forbid
That I suould justifie you.
It was the Justification of his friends uhich his soule did soab¬
hor. To justifie some men is a dutie, and there are many men
(I grant) whom to justifie were a fin. There is a sinfull judging
of others, concerning which Christ saith (Math. 7. 1.) Judg not,
that ye be not judged. They who judge others unjustly, shall be
iustly judged. There is also a sinfull justifying of others. They
who justifie others unduely, may expect condemnation as their
due. But were Tobs friends such as could not be justified without
sin? could he not justifie them, without deserving to be condem¬
ned himselfe? Did he jadge them hypocrites, as they judged him,
and so not to be justified? I conceive not, surely he did not judge
them wicked, and doubtlesse they were not, as hath been shewed
before; how is it then that he saith, God forbid that I should justifie
you? I ansver, we must restrain this act of justification to the cause
or case in hand, it doth not refer to their persons, but to their dis¬
pute. God forbid that I should justifie you in this, in your Judgment
of me, in the opinion you have taken up of me, or in the sensure
ye have given of me. Ye hive cast me as an evil-doer, but I can¬
not subscribe to your sentence; God forbid that I should justifie you
Chap. 27. An Exposition apon the Book of JO2.
in this. So then, Job dotn not speak of them as of reprobites,
whom God had not brought, nor would bring into a state of ju¬
stification;but he speaks of them as having spoken and done such
things as ought to be reprobated, or disapproved by all good men,
and which no man ought to justifie. Job medled not either with
the constant course of their lives, or the state of their souls, he
went no further than what concerned the present disputation;God
forbid that I should justifie you in that.
But how doth man justifie man? is it not God that justifieth?
as the Apostle Paul speaks (Rom. 8. 53.) How then doth Tob
speak, as if he had pouer to justifie ? I answer, as before, Jobs
words are not to be understood of the justification of their persons
before God,but of the justification of their actions towards him,
before man; God forbid that I should justifie you; that is, that I should
affirm that to be true of me, which ye my friends affirm to be
true, or that ye have dealt friendly, according to the rule of truth
with me. We justifie a man, when, what he affirms we stand to.
or when we say that thing is well done which he hath done, or that
he hath done well in doing it, this is to justifie him. Man justifieth
man, when he affirms that to be true which he saith, and that to
be good which he doth; ot that he hath done and spoken nothino
but what is good and true. No man can either justifie or cou¬
demn another, as to the determining of his state, but we may
upon just grounds) either condemne or justifie another, as to
the approving or disapproving of his way.
Thus Job professeth he will not justifie his friends, he will not
say as they said, nor think well ot what they had done; he could
not doit, he would not do it till he dyed (as he speaks in the
next clause) that is, he would never do it.
Hence Observe;
First, ue may and must judge of men, as they are and do.
We must both justifie and condemn as ve see, or according
what appeares. Mans justification of man, must proceed upon
other terms than Gods justification of man doth. God justifieth
the ungodly ( Rom. 4. 5.) But woe to those men who justifie the
ungodly; God would not justifie the ungodly, but for the righte¬
ousnesse of another; and shall we justifie the ungodly in then
own unrighteousnesse? Whomsoever we justifie, must first be

0056.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book ot JOR. Verf.5.

body.t: just, our justification cannot make him so. As the termes of Gods
electing man are quite different from those upon which man ought
to elect or choose, so also are they in justification; God electeth
those in whom he seeth no good, nor doth he elect any for their
goodnesse, either because he seeth them good, or foreseeth the
will be good. He beholdeth no excellency, beauty, ot w orthi¬
nesse in them; He elects according to the pleasure of his own
will, mans goodnesse is not the cause, but the effect of Gods e¬
lection: The election of God maketh men good, it doth find them.
so. But if man elects, he must elect those that are good, those that
have somewhat in them to commend them tohim; He must choose
them because they are learned and Skilfull in reference to the im¬
ployments and bufinesses, to which they are called, or because
he seeth they are honest, sober, gracious; man must not elect, as
God elects, neither must he justifie as God justifies; therefore
saith Tob) God forbid I should jastifie you; I must speak plainely
according to what I find you. Solomon hath given us the deter¬
mination of this poynt in full and downe-right language (Pro.17.
15.) He that justifieth the micked, and he that condemneth the righ¬
ttous, even they both are abomination to the Lord. Of which wicked
practice rhe Lord complaines by the prophet (Ezck. 13.19.)
will re pollute me among my people for handfulls of Barley, and for
pieces of bread, to slay the souls that should not dye ( that is, to con¬
demne the righteous ) and to save the souls alive that should not
live (that is, to justifie the wicked) by your lying to my people, that
heare your lyes. God justifieth whom he will, man must justifie
according tothe will of God.
Secondly, Considering that Jobs freinds were ( as to their
state) godly and righteous persons, such as God justisied, and
yet fob said well; God forbid that I should justifie you.
Note;
We must not justifie a good man, when he doth evill, or in that
mbich he doth ill.
A good man, a man justified in the sight of God, may doe a¬
misse in the sight of man, and in that he ought not to be justified
by man. We must not justifie any man in any one evill action,
because he hath done many thit are good. As it is very sinful for
any man to justifie and defend any evill that he hath done, so it

0057.head: Chap.27. An Exposition apon the Book of JOR. Verf.5

body.t: as sinfull to justifie others, or to be their advocates when they
have done evill, or in any evill deed. Every action must be weigh¬
ed by it selfe, and stand upon its owne bottom, one cannot helpe
or save another. It is our dutie to forgive another, many ill car¬
riages and uncharitable, yea injurious actings towards us, but to
justifie them, or him in them, would be our sin. In all such cases
let us say, God for bid I should justifie you, though you may be such
as God justifieth, and though ye have done many things w hich
are not onely justifiable, but commendable in another kinde.
Christ knew that Peter was a holy man for the maine, yet when he
gave him ill counsell, he turned and said unto him, Get thee behind
me Satan, thou art an offence to me, for thou savour est not ( in this
thing) the things that be of God, but those that be of men (Math, 16.
22.) And we read that the Apostle Paul was so farre from justi¬
fying the Apostle Peter himselfe, when he saw, that through his
fault, many walked not uprightly, according to the truth of the Go¬
spel, that (saith he) I witbstood him to the face, because he mas to be
blamed, ( Gal. 2.11, 14.) We cannot doe better for our best
friends, than to let them know when they doe badly. Nor should
we for any thing more condemne our selves, than for justifying
another in any thing for which he ought to be condemned. Goa
forbid that I should justifie you.
Till I dye I will not remove mine integrity from mi.
In this latter part of the verse, Job gives a reason of what hesaid
the former ; He could not justifie them without removing, or
parting wirh his owne integrity, which was the best Jewel he had
the world, and which he was resolved ne ver to part with while
he lived. Therefore, saith he,
Tih I dye, &c.
The Originall word notes an easie, a quiet, a naturall death;
though I should live till my candle doth consume away, and spend
it self, not being violent ly blowne out by others; though I should
live as long as I could live, I could not justifie you, God forbid
should justifie you, till I dye, &c. There is a double cont xion of
these words, till I dye, The Greeke Inte:preters joyne them to the
antecedent words, the Latines to those which follow, till I dye
mill not remove my integrity from me;but it is not of concernment

0058.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verf.5.

body.t: whether? we connect them toformer or latter, or divide them be¬
tween both, I mill not justifie you till I dye, neither will I, till
dye, remove mine integrity from me.
TillI dye
The meaning is not, that Job would remove his integrity at or
before his death, but this is a strong affirmition that he would
never remove it;I will not doe it till I dye, is, I will not doe it
at all.
We may give a twofold interpretation of this his resolution,
vill not dot it till I dye. First thus, as if he were resolved not to doc
this, though it should cost him his life;he esteemed his integrity at
such a rate, that he could easier lay down his life than let goe his
integrity. Life is the best of Naturals, but integrity is the best of
moralls and spiritualls; and therefore though he dyed for it, he
would not ( by any act or concession of his) remove, no nor ble¬
mish his integrity. As if he had said; though I knew my life were
your hands,and ye able to take my life from me, yet I would not
doe this thing, I am fixed and at a poynt with you in this, what
ever it cost me. And because this sence is much insisted upon by
some, it being a truth, and complying with other Scriptures.
Observe;
A Gelly man resolveth he mill never dot evill, comt of it what will,
Fall back or fall edge,he will not doe it. A godly man resolves
against doing that which is an evill of wrong to others, much more
against doing that which is an evill both of wrong and sin to him¬
selfe. Zealous Daniel was thus resolved when he saw he could not
preserve his integrity without endangeringthe life of another,
which could no but be extreamly dangerous to himselfe. (Dan. 1.
8.) Daniel purposed in his heart that he mould not defile himselfe
with the portion of the Kings meat, nor mith the mine mhich he
drank, therefore he requested of the Prince of the Eunuchs that he
might not defile himselfe. Aad the Prince of the Eunuchs said unto
Daniel, I feare my Lord the King, who hath appoynted your meat
and your drinbe, for why should he see your faces worse libing than
the children which are of your sort, then shall ye mabe me endanger my
bead to the king. Daniel might well thinke, This Great officer
would not easily grant him a favour which in the issue might

0059.head: Chap.27. An Exposition apon the Book Jof JOR. Verf.5

body.t: lose him not only the Kings favour, but his head too. Courtiers
doe not use to be free of such favours, especially to poore Cap¬
tives, who hive no meanes to oblige them; yet Daniel put it to
venture; purposing in his heart to abstaine from all uncleane
whether meates or drinkes, what e’re came on’t. And as the God¬
Iy are or should be alwayes resolved not to doe any evill, though
they dye for it, so they resolve sometimes to doe this or that good,
though they dye for it; they will run all hazzards rather than for¬
beare a knowne present duty in its season. That magnanimoue
woman, Hester, said, If I perifh I perish, it is my duty, at such a time
as this, I see it is my duty, I am resolved, I will goe in to the King
mhich is not according to the Law, and if I perish I perish, (Hest.4.
16.) When Paul sawit was a duty to goe to Jerusalem, he was
resolute against all suggestions of dangers, But none of these things
move me, neither account I my life deare to my selfe, that I might
finish my course witb joy (Acts. 20. 24.) As if Paul had said (
great man once did) It is necessary for me to goe, but it is not
necessary for me to live; and therefore goe I will though I dye
for it. And as he was fixed against all the dangers which the ene¬
my at Jerusalem threatned him with, so against all those disswa¬
sives with which his friends endeavoured to take him off from the
purpose of his intended journeyto Jerusalem (Acts 21. 11, 12,
13,14.) When Agabus a Prophet had taken Pauls girdle and
bound his omne hands and feet, saying, thus saith the Holy Ghost,
shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle;
The Disciples hearing these things, added their exhortation to his
prædicton, and besought him not to goe up to Jerusalem; Then Paul
ansmered, mbat meane ye to metpe and to breake mine heart? for I am
ready not onelyto be bound but to Iye at Jerusalem for the name
the Lord Jesus. True courage delights in the ayre of thit danger
where duty dwels, and will neither be beaten off from doing an
incumbent duty, nor beaten on to doe any thing against a duty by
the reports or appearances of the greatest perill. To be thus re¬
solved is an heroick, and noble resolution indeed. As a wicked man
will sin, so a godly man saith he will not sin, though he dye. He
chooseth the worst of afflictions rather than iniquity.
Secondly, we may take these words, till I dye, in a milder
sence; though it was in the breast of Tob to dye rather than to do
this, yet I will not doe this till I dye, may here carry in it no more
than this, I will not doe it as long as I live.

0060.head: Chap.27. An Expositon mpon the Boik of JOB. Verf.5.

body.t: Hence Observe;
A godly man is everlastingly resolved, and set against sin,
In this case he makes no temporary promises, he doth not pur¬
pose to forbeare sin for a time, much lesse till he hath a fit time,
but for ever. Some will not sin for a time, and they forbeare one¬
Iy till they have a fit time to sin. All the reason why some doe no
evill is because they cannot, or because they have not an opportu¬
nity to doe it. Falix said to Paul, Got thy way for this time, when
bave a convenient season I will send for thet; so say they of their sin,
at a convenient time I will doe it. There is neither time nor sei¬
son allowed or appoynted by God for sin, and therefore we must
not give our selves allowance for it at any time or season. We
should (as was shewed before ) rather choose to dye than to sin,
how much more should we resolve, not to sin till we dye.
Till Idye,
I will not remove my integrity from me.
The word signifies to yeild or give bick, to remove, or cause
give back; Thus saith Tob, I will not yeeld up my integrity,or,
will not cause my integrity to give back. The word which we
render integrity, signifieth also perfection, and simplicity, that is,
religious, plain, honest and simple disposition, without guile or
wickedness, or (as we say) without welt or guard. In the breast¬
plate of Aaron, there was the Urim, and the Thummim, which lat-
ter is this word; Job had the true Thummim in his Breast, and he
would not remove it.
Hence Note;
A godly man is a man of integrity.
He hath Urim and Thummim, as well as the High-Priest had,
he hath his light of truth or his fire of zeale, and he hath his per¬
fection, or integrity, both in his breast, and upon his breast. These
are seated as heavenly principles in his heart, and they are held
forth in the course and practices of his life, as a light shining from
heaven.
Note, Secondly;
Integrity is, in it selfe, a thing of great price.
We can easily part with or remove those things which are not

0061.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verf.5.

body.t: of worth. Integrity is plaine and simple, yet the best ornament
and decking ( next Christ) of the whole man. Solomon in all his
outward glory was not arrayed like one of these lillyes. We are
nevir so fine as whex me are plaine. To be plaine, simple, to have
spirit without tricks and turnings, without knots and riddles,
better and more honourable, than the highest titles of honour,
Integrity is our perfection under the Covenant of Grace, and sim¬
plicit yis our greatest excellency. Tis the fundamentall excellency
of God himselfe, and so it is of his people. That which is truely
simple is truely perfect in its kinde, and therefore the same word
signifies both simple, and perfect ; this is the Glory of Grice,
and the Grace of Glory. How Glorious are we when this pre¬
cious stone of integrity, this spirituall Thummim fixed in our
hearts, sparkleth in all our wayes.
Thirdly, Observe;
A Godly man is acquainted with his owne integrity.
He knows he hath this Jewell about him, though others see
not, he doth; possibly a godly man may sometimes suspect him¬
selfe to be a hypocrite, (for as there are some hypocrites, who
think themselves to be sincere, all are not grosse, or selfe con¬
demned hypocrites, so it is possible for some whoare sincere to
judg themselves hypocrites) yet take a Codly man out of the
clouds and darknesse of temptation, or desertion, and then as he
wbat he appeares to others, so he appears to himselfe as he is,
sincere and full of integrity.
Fourthly, Observe;
A godly man priz eth his integrity higbly.
What a man will not remove and part with, surely he reckons
as his best. That which is worthlesse, filthy, or uncleane, as dung
we take away as dung, till it be all gone (as ’tis said ) 1 Kings. 14.
10. ) take it who will; but our treasures, our jewells, we will not
part with. The reason why a carnall man will not remove his ipi¬
quity from him, is because he values it and lookes upon it either
as his pleasure, or as his profit. This makes him hold it fast, as
the Prophet complaines (Jer.8.5.) They hold fast deceit. We say
proverbially, and we say it truely, Plaine dealing is a Jewell; bue
with some, Deceit or false dealing is a Jewell, and therefore they

0062.head: Chip.27. An Expositon npon the Bock of JOE. Vers.5.

body.t: hold it fast, and will not let it goe. Whatsoever it is, whether
good or bad, which we will not remove, nor suffer ( if we can
helpe it) to be removed fromus, that’s our Jewell, that's hioh¬
prized, and much esteemed by us. Our integrity is, our all, next
Christ, and Christ is nothing to those who have no integrity. It
said of a Womin, That having lost her modesty, she hath nothing
more to lose. And it is most true both of man and woman; They
have nothing more to lose than their integrity; How highly
should we prize that without which all that we have besides is ot
no price at all?
Fifthly, Observe;
A godly man should doe nothing in prejudice to his integrity.
Not to remove integrity,is lesse than not to throw away inte¬
grity, it is to doe nothing that may staine, or lay the least blott
upon it. They who are fullest of integrity, are often blotted by
others; the dirt of hypocrisie is throwne in their faces, while their
hearts are upright with God, and their wayes towards men. How
common is it to object that which doth not appear, when nothing
appeares to object. Thus others remove the integrity of the most
upright. But how sad is it for an upright man to doe that which
may staine his owne integrity, and render him not only suspected
but blotted. That which was fobs great care should be ours, not
move in any thing which may remove our integrity. God up¬
boldeth his people in their integrity ( Psal.41. 12.) How steddily
then should his people hold their integriry. Let integrity and up¬
rightness preserve me, was Davids prayer (Psal, 25.21.) O let us
preserve our integrity and uprightness; What shall me preserve,
not our preservers!
Sixthly, Note;
He that admits of any false accusation or wrong judgment a¬
gainst himself, removes or staines bis owne Integrity.
We must stand our ground, and be stiffe for our selves against
all mis-judgings. It is good to be zealously affected alwayes in¬
good matter, whether it respects the glory of God immediitely
and alone, or whether it respect the credit of our brethren, or our
owne. To desire to be famous in the world, and (as those Giants
in the old world, (Gen. 6.4.) men of renowne, or (as the origi¬

0063.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition apon the Book of JOR. Verf.6.

body.t: nal text hath it) men of name, is a very great vanity, but to pro¬
tect and preserveur good name, is a great and necessary duty.
Job though it so necessary, that he was not satisfied with affirm¬
ing this once, but doubles the same affirmation, though in other
words.
Verse 6. My righteousnesse I hold fast, I will not let it goe, my
heart shall not reproach me so long as l live.
This verse is filled with the spirit of the former; Job here also
shewing the steadfastness of his purpose to insist upon his innocen¬
cy, and keepe it close, against all assaults of enemies, or suspitions
of friends. Though they pulled, yet he would hold fast.
Ay righteousnesse I hold fast.
The Hebrewis, Upon my righteousnesse I hold strongly, or, I mill
fortifie and strengthen my righteousnesse. The righteousnesse of
man may be considered two wayes; either in reference to justifi¬
cation, or sanctification; and this righteousnesse ot sanctification
may be considered two wayes: first, as it is the righteousnesse of
mans person, or that principle of righteousnesse implanted and
inbærent in him; Secondly, as it is the righteousnesse of his acti¬
ons, or that practice of righteousnesse which is held out by him,
That which Job intends here by righteousnesse, is not the righte¬
ousnesse of justification, but the righteousnesse of sanctification,
and not so much the righteousnesse of his person, as of his actions
or cause in this engagement with his friends. My righteousnesse
bold fast. A believer doth not hold fast his righteousnesse in refe¬
rence to justification, there he letteth it goe, he will have nothing
to do withit, he will not owne it. Paul while a Pharisee held fast
his own righteousnesse for Justification, but being converted,
Christ taught him better Divinity ( Phil. 3. 6, 7, 8, 9.) Touch¬
ing the righteousnesse which is in the Law I was blamelesse. But what
things mere gaine to me, (that is, what I then counted gaine as to
my acceptation with God] those I counted lesse for Christ; that is,
let them goe, and they were as lost to me, that I might take fast
hold of Christ, and beare my selfe, or, lay the whole weight of my
Justification, upon him alone, as he expounds himselfe in the next
verse; Tea doubtlesse, and I count all things but dung and drosse for
the excellency of the knomledg of Christ Jesus my Lord; for mhom

0064.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Vers.6.

body.t: bave suffered the losse of all things, and dot count them but dung
that l may min Christ, and be found in him, not having my own
rigbteousnesse, mhich is of the Lax. As if he had said, I would not
be found to have any of my oun righteousnesse in my hand for
world; For as to the businesse of justification, our righteousnesse
drosse and dung, yea, all our righteousnesses are as filthy raggs,
(Ila. 14. 6.) Not only are those righteous acts filthy which are
done (as the Pharisees did theirs) for self-ends,or in hypocrisie,
but there is a filthinesse (as they are done by us) in those righte¬
ous acts which are done to a right end, or in sincerity; and there¬
fore the most righteous person must not hold his righteousnesse,
he must let it goe. Though I were rigbteous (saith Tob, Ch.9.15.)
jet would I not ansmer, (in a legal way for justification in my selfe)
but I mould make supplication to my Judge; that is, I would hum¬
ble my selfe and begge his pardon. And again (v. 21.) Though
mere perfect, yet would I not know my omn soul. But when it com¬
eth to a case or controversie between him and his friends, then he
held fast his righteousnesse, the righteousnesse of his sanctification
and conversation. There, righteousnesse is no drosse, but gold, sil¬
ver, precious stones, the souls riches; of this righteousnesse fob
professeth in the present Text, I hold it fast. The word signifies
hold strongly; As if he had said, This my righteousness I hold
with all my strengtb; no man shall take it from me, but I’le know
wby. This steddy purpose of Tob here repeated may import two
things.
First, Persevetance in doing righteously; As if he had said,
mill never give over the mayes and worbs of righteousnesse. Thus
the Lord bespeaks Satan (Ch. 2.3.) Hast thou considered my ser¬
vant Job, that there is none libe bim in the earth, a perfect man, and
an uprigbt, one that feareth God, and escheweth evill, and stil he
boldetb fast his intagrity, although thou movedst me against him
destroy bim witbout cause. When the Lord said, be holdeth fast bis
integrity, the meaning is, he persevereth, or goeth on, acting his
integrity; he will not be beiten off, no not by all these blowes:
Thou hast moved me to destroy him, but destruction it selt can¬
not remove him from his duty. So some expound the place here,
my righteousnesse l hold fast; as if Job would shew, that as he had
kept, so he wis purposed to keep a perpetual course ot holinesse,
righteousnesse and justice, from the very first to the last; but

0065.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOR. Verf.6.

body.t: conceive this is not the proper interpretation of this place. The
word which we translate, I bold fast, doth not so much imply per¬
severance in doing righteously, as the defence and maint enance of
what he had done, to be righteous, or of the right which he had
done; my righteousness I hold fast, I maintain it, I stand to it;
and he speaks in the present tense noting a continued act through
all time. He doth not say, I have held it fast, or mill hold it fast,
but I hold it fast, as with my very teeth. Job is not treating of
his perseverance in righteous wayes, but affirming that his wayes
had been righteous, though his suspitious friends suggested other¬
wise.
My righteousnesse I hold fast.
The Emphasis of the word here rendred, Hold fast, reaches
little further than hath yet been signified, even to hold witha
kind of obstinicy or pertinacy of spirit; it notes such a holding
as takes incouragement by opposition: which the more it is assaul¬
ted to let goe, the more it is engaged to hold. That speech of
Christ (Luke 19. 15.) attains this sence fully. And it came te
passe (saith the Evangelist ) that w ben the time mas come that Christ
should be received up, be stedfastly set bis face to goe to Terusalem;
the Greek is, he hardened or strengthened bis face; The Syriack
saith, He prepared himself to got, (that which we firmly purpose
doe, we prepare to doe) Christ would rot be diverted by any
advise, counsel, or perswasion, but the time being come, that he
should be received up, that he should suffer, and enter into glory,
he stedfastly set his face, he was irrevocably set to goto Jerusalem,
He prepared himself, though he knew what a bitter cup was pre¬
paring for him, and that he must passe through the valley of the
shadow of death. Thus Job hardened his face, and was invincibly
resolved to stand to his tackling, my righteousness I hold fast,
And will not let it goe.
That’s the Negative of the former Affirmative; when a man
resolved to hold any thing fast, he mill not let goe; there is an ele¬
gancy in the expression. The original word fignifies to be weake
or infirme. To let a thing go, or to remit lit, shews a werknesse
him that doth so, and so this word is properly opposed to that
the former clause, to holding fast. In this sence we read it

0066.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOR. Vers.6.

body.t: Pro. 18. 9.) He also that is sloathful in his work, is brother
him that is a great waster. The slothful man is weak at his
work, he will easily let it go, his work drops out of his hand,
or from between his fingers. What we do not set our hearts to,
we care not to set our hands to, or hold it in our hearts. That Scri¬
pture ( Num. 13. 18.) will give us a little more light about the
force of this word. When Moses sent out the spies, and gave them
instructions what they should doe in the Land of Canaan; See
saith he) mbat the people are, mhether they be strong or meak, fen
many, learne or enforme your selves, whether they be a people
that will easily part with their Land, and give up the hold of their
possessions. Cousider whether they be strong, and valiant men,
that will dispute and fight for every patch of ground ere they part
with it, or whether they be weak, that is, such as will easily let
their Land goe, and be turned out of all their labours, to save
themselves a labour. The word is used also in the story of the Le¬
vite (Tudg. 19.9.) And mhen the man rose up to depart, he and his
Concubine, and his Servant, his Father in Law, the damsels father
said unto him, behold now the day drameth tomards evening; the He¬
brew is, as we put in the Margin of our larger Bibles, the day is
weak, or ready to let the Light go; in the morning the light m¬
creaseth and waxeth stronger and stronger, but towards evening
the day or the Light is going away, it groweth weak when the Sun
departeth. Now, saith fob, I will not let go mine integrity, my in¬
tegrity shall be as the ascending or morning Sun, climbing higher
and higher, my integrity shall not decline or go down, I will
not let it go, but it shall shine brighter and brighrer, till it shineth
forth in full ftrength. And in this sense Tacob spake to the Angel,
(Gen.32.24.) whomade request, Lit me got, for the day breab¬
eth, no, saith Jacob, I will not let thet goe except thou blesse me.
And thus saith Tob, I mill not let it goe: I will net act like a weak
man, what I have undertaken I will abide by, and not give an inch
of ground. As Moses said to Pharaoh about the departure of Is¬
rael (Exod. 10.26,) Our cattel shall go with us, there shall not an
honfebe left behind, I will not let any thing go that belongs to Is¬
rael. Thus constant is Tob in this controversie, about his righte¬
ousnesse, he would not lose a hair of it. I will not let
goc.
I 2

0067.head: Chap. 27. An Expofition upon the Book of JOE. Verf.6.

body.t: Hence Observe;
As a godly man resolves to bold onin the prastice of righteousnesse
against all temptation, so to maintain bis righteousnesse against
all oppofition.
He that knoweth he is sincere, cannot be perswaded, nor bea¬
ten from holding his sincerity: a godly min (as the Apostle
Tames describes the wisdome from above, that is, those who are
made wise from above, Chap. 3. 17.) is first pure, then peaceable,
gentle, and easit to be entreated. He may be intreated easily in some
things, but in others you may as soon remove a rocke as move
him, there’s no intreating, no perswading him; a godly man
easily entreated to do good for others, and he is easily intreated
to remit the wrong which others have done him; in these tyo ca¬
ses he is easily entreated : but if you come to take his integrity
from him, and touch him in his uprightuesse, he will by no means
be intreated to wrong himself. As it is finful (in many cases)
not to remit the wrong done to us by others, so not to maintaine
the right done by our selves; we may, yea we ought sometimes
for peace sake) to part with our right; but we may not, we must
not part with our righteousnesse: for that indeed is as, if not more
sinful, than to wrong others; to beare false witnesse against our
selves is the falsest witnesse-bearing; In mbat ve are houest and in¬
nocent, we cannot be too stout. He buyes his peace too deare, who
either quits the truth of God for it, or the truth ot his own
wayes. It is dangerous laying down our own will, to submit to
any thing which is not according to the will of God. Here and
no where else wilfulnesse is a vertue. I will not let it ge, saith Tob,
and he did well in saying so, for else he had fallen into the after¬
claps, indeed, the thunder-claps of his own conseience, which he
had no mind to doe, as he professeth in the next words.
Mi beart shall not reproach me so long as I live.
That is, my couscience shall not; the heart in Scripture is put
for the understanding, for the will, for the affections, as hath been
elsewhere shewed, here for the conscience; my heart shall not re¬
proach me. To reproach, is to cast a blot upon our selves or others,
The original word is sometimes translated to blaspheme (Isa.65.
7.) Blasphemy is the highest degree of reproach. Joh speakes here

0068.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Vers.6.

body.t: to his friends dealing with him; as it he had said, Te my friends
bave repreached me often, but I am resolved my own haart shall not
reproach me. He tells them (Chap.19.3.) thise ten timas have ye
reproached me; but reproich ye as long and as often as ye will, my
heart shall not reproich me once or at all, if I can avoyd it, as
long as I live.
There is a double rendring of these words; some give them in
the time past, Ay heart hath not reproached me all my dayes, er all
the time that I have lived; That is a very good sense: Job was ot
such integrity, that though he had many failings, yet he had not
sinned against the dictates of his conscience, and so had not bro¬
ken his peace by what he had done, though he had often donc
that which called him to repentance. Our Transsation, and so ge¬
nerally others, read the words in the future tense, My heart shall
not reproach me, I will not give it cause to reproich me, which
should doe, if I should assent to your reproiches, My heart spall
not reproach me as long as I live; The Hebrew is, from my dayes;
which hath a double interpretation; First, concerning my dayes;
that is, concerning my manner of living Master Broughton seemes
comply with this reading as best, My heart shall take no shame
from my dayes, that is, from those things which I have done in my
dayes, or from my whole conversation; not as if he thought him¬
self free from sin, but he had not gone on knowingly in a way ot
sinning, or he had not acted against his knowledge. We cannot
but doe that which we know to be sinful, and yet, possibly, we
may not sin against our knowledge. Secondly, From my dayes,
that is, all the dayes that either I have, or shall live. This form of
speaking being used indifferently, both in reference to the time
past, and to come, is a confirmation of Tobs integrity; he had so
lived that his confcience did not check him, and he was resolved
to go on, with so much clearnesse, that his conscience should
have no cause to check him, !My heart shall not reproach me as long
I livt,
Hence Observe;
First, Conscience, or the heart of man, bath an accusing, or an up¬
braiding poner in it.
Conscience is a very busie faculty of the soul, and it hath many
offices. First, Conscience is as a register to take notice of and re¬

0069.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verf,6.

body.t: cord what we do. Secondly, Conscience is a witnesse against us,
or an accuser, when we do amiss. Thirdly, Conscience is a Judg,
and gives the sentence (1 John 3. 20.) If our heart condemn us,
God is greater than our heart, and bnoneth all things; if our heart
condemn us not, then have me confidence towards God. Conscience
sits upon a Throne as Gods deputy, to auard life or death. Fourth¬
Iy, Conscience hath the office of a tormenter, it is that worme
which dyeth not, and a fire that never goeth out. The damned
shall feele the teeth and sting of conscience for ever, though here
they have brib’d it, and blinded it, that it might not trouble them.
The work of conscience intended in this Text is the second, the
accusing and witnessing work of conscience. He thit accuseth
another, reproacheth him, and every accusation is a reproich,
it be false ’tis a reproach till it is removed, and if it be true tis
reproich that cannot be removed. Of this work of Couscience
the Apostle speaks (Rom. 2. 15.) Which shew the worke of the
Law written in their hearts, their consciences also bearing witnesse,
and their thoughts the mean mhile accusing or else excusing one
another. Though the lives of carnal men oppose the Law, yet the
conscience of the most wicked min in the world doth comply
and corre pond with the Law, to bind or to loose him, to accuse
or excuse him upon the view of what he hath done.
Secondly, Observe;
An enlightned and awakered conscience, xill vex and upbraia
those that do evil.
Many have done as much and more, than Tob saith here he would
not do, lest his conscience should reproach him, & yet their consci¬
ences never reproached them for it; the y have silenced their own
consciences, or through ignorance, their consciences have not lear¬
ned to speak, and so they sin, and conscience saith nothing; They
who are alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that
them, (as the Apostle speaks, Eph. 4. 18.) may and doe live
like devils in a course of wickednesse, and never receive so much
as one check from conscience; yea, the reason why many desire
to have no light in their conscience, is, because they would not be
under the rebukes of conscience. A blind sleepy conscience will
let a man sin, and sin a thousand times, and ¿never give him an ill
word; but if a Job, a man of an enlighened conscience sin, his con¬

0070.head: Chap.27. An Expositon npon the Boett ef JOR. Verf.6.

body.t: science will be upon him presently, and tell him his own. There¬
fore he said, My conscience shall not reproach me; I know it will,
should do evil; it is possible for an ill man to hive a good con¬
science in its kind, that is, a conscience naturally good, though not
morally good; for when conscience doth its office, it is a nitural
good conscience. Tne office of conscience is to reproich us when
we do evil ; A wicked mans conscience may do that, it may tell
him, he hath done this or that sinful evil, and fo deserves this or
that penal evil. Again, it is possible for a godly man to hive
an ill conscience (in this sense) that is, a conscience which doth
not its office, as to some particular, his conscience may be afleep,
or not enlightned in some things; his conscience may be much out
of order, and unfit for the exercise and discharge of its proper du¬
ty. When David had committed those horrible sins of adultery,
and murther, his conscience was discomposed and off the hinges
for a whole yeare, it never reproached him, he wis as a stranger to
his own bosome; till his sin was discovered to him, it troubled
him not. But when Nathan came to him and ( having made him
give sentence against another man in a Parable) told him plainly,
thou art the man, his conscience quickly gave sentence against him¬
self, and he confessed, I have sinned against the Lord (2Sim. 12.13.)
Nothing besides the blood of Christ, can stop the voyce and still
the cry of an awakened conscience. But being once thus purged,
we have no mort conscience of sins (Heb. 10.2.) that is, so more
rebukes and reproiches of conscience for sin. They who know they
are pardoned in Christ, make conscience of committing the least
sin, but they have no conscience of the greatest sins committed.
Thirdly, Observe;
A godly! man is afraid of the chidings and upbraidings ofhis
ows conscience.
It is better to have the reproiches of all the men in the world
fall upon us, than the reproiches of conscience, better that all the
men in the world should call us hypocrite and wicked, than that
conscience should tell us so; a godly man fears the accusation
and sentence of his conscience, next to the judgment and sentence
of God himself. Yes natural men many times are much afraid
ot their consciences, and do therefore eschew evil, lest conscience
should trouble them, and upon the same terms they do good.

0071.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Vers.6́

body.t: They find if they should omit such a duty, if they should not som¬
times pray, and hear the Word, they must answer it to their con¬
sciences. This is a true distinction between a godly and a carnal
man; a godly man doth good, not for feare his conscience should
trouble him, but because his conscience is pleased with, and suited
the doing of good. Yet conscience is terrible to a good man
when he sins, as wellas to a wicked, even he is afraid of the chid¬
ings of conscience; therefore as Paul saith in reference to civil
Magistrates (Rom. 13. 3.) so I say in reference to that natural
Magistrate in your breasts, conscience, Wilt thou then not be afraid
the power, do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the
same. The Magistrite is a terrour, not to good works, but to evill
workes; conscience is a Magistrate within, and that is a terrour,
not to good works,but to evil; therefore my advice is, would ye
not be afraid of the power ot conscience, do that which is good,
and ye shall have praise ot the same, that is, your conscience will
commend you, or give testimony for you : it is sweet, no man
knows how sweet but he that hath it, to have the testimony of
good conscience upon good grounds; A flattering from consci¬
ence is the soarest curse, but a true testimony from consci¬
ence is an unspeakable mercy. Doe good, and ye shall have
good words, and a good witness from conscience.
Fourthly, Observe;
A godly man is very careful not to give his conscience any ecca¬
sion to reproach bim.
Whatsoever he doth, or what shift soever he makes,he will not
doe any thing which may put him in the hand of conscience to
schoole and chide him; that is the tendency of all. When Job said,
rconscience shall not reproach me, his meaning was, I will not
doe that which shall render me naked and lyable to the reproi¬
ches of conscience. It is impossible to avoyde the reproiches of
conscience, unlesse we avoyde and turne from that which putsa
word of reproach in the mouth of conscience. Sin puts not only
word, but a sword in the mouth of conscience to wound us,
therefore a godly man, next to his care that he give not God an
occasion against him, will not give his conscience an occasion a¬
gainst him. Conscience acts in subordination to Cod. A good
conscience is as a Paradise, it makes musick within; conscience is

0072.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon tbe Book of JOR. Verf.6́.

body.t: pleasant bird, it sings sweetly, and when conscience sings sweet¬
Iy, we are fittest to act vigorously. Conscience is a book, for
the mending of the faults whereof allother books have been
made; and when once conscience is mended and set right, so that
we can say in truth as Paul (Acts 23.1. )uu have livedin all
good conscience hefore God, and (as he speakes in another place of
