that booke) have kept our consciences void of offence both tomards
Gol and towards man, then have we confidence both towards
God, and towards man, and have good ground to say, Our heart
shall not reproach us as long as we live,
A good or pure couscience( as other Scriptures eall it )will cer¬
tainely be a quiet & a peaceable conscience;a good conscience will
not only not reproich or trouble us, but ir will exceedingly re¬
tresh and comfort us. So the Apostle professed from his own
experience (2 Cer. 1. 12.) Our rejoycing is this, the testinony
our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not mith fleshly
wisdome, but by the grace of God, ve have had our conversation in
the world, and more abundantly to jou-wards. When conscience
beares its testimony with us, and for us, how full of joy is the
soul, even in the midst of many outward sorrows? And is trou¬
ble of conscience is the greatest trouble, so joy of conscience is the
greatest joy. That man can never want musick, whose conscience
speakes in consort, and is harmonious with himself. A good con¬
science is the poore mans riches,and the rich mans Jewel; A good
conscience is the best pillow to fleepe upon, and the best dish to
feed upon. A dish, said I? ’tis a feast; A feast, said I? Solomon
saith more (Pro. 15. 15. )’tis a continuall feast? The Geneva
tranflation saith, A gool couscienct, ours, a merry heart (which doth
not contradict the other, but explaine it. A good and a merry
heart or conscience ) is a continuall feast. And as they who are
merry are fit for a feast, so at a feast tis both proper and comely
be merry. And while conscience continues good, the feast uill
continue, and therefore a good conscience must needs be a conti¬
nuall feast. Nor is it to play the Epicure, to be alwayes at this
feast; for in this feast every pot and dish is Holiness totbe Lord. Nor
shall any need to feare a surfet, by being continually at this feast;
for as the feasters are temperate, so their appetite and a isfaction
are perpetually interchangable. They shall be alwayes feasted by
conscience, who areca refull that their consciences shall not at all
K

0073.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bock ef JO». Verf.7.

body.t: reproich them; this was Jobs resolution; My, conscience shall not
reproach me so long as I live.
JOB, Chap. 27. Vers.7,8.
Let mine Enemy be as the miched, and he that riseth up
against me, as the unrighteous.
For mhat is the hope of the hypocrite, though he have
gained, mhen God taheth away his soul?
N the former verse, we found Tob holding fast and stifly main¬
Ataining his own righteousnesse, against all the objections and
jealousies of his friends; in this he cither fastneth unrighreousness
or the reward of the unrighteous, upon his Enemy, or opposer;
Let mine Enemy be as the wiek ed, and he that riseth up against me,
as the unrighteous.
Let Nine Enemy.
Somé tender and expound the words, not as a wish or desire,
but as a Prophesie; in which fob foretelleth what would become
of his Enemy, or what evill should befall him : Mine Enemy shall
be asthe mich ed, & he that risetb up against me as the unrigbteous.
But I rather take it ( according to our reading) for an impreca¬
tion, or wish, that evill might come upon his Enemy.
Let mine enemy be as the micked.
What a wicked min is, and the force ot the originallword here
used, hath been opened heretofore, therefore I shall not stay upon
it. Both parts of this verse are of one sence and meaning: that
which he saith in the beginning (Let mine Enemy be as the mic¬
led) he speaks againe in the close of this verse (and he that ri¬
setb upagainst me, as the unrigbteous. This latter is but a reinforce¬
ment of the same thing in a different forme and shape of words,
He that riseth up against me.
This riser is none othet, than his Enemy before spoken of; yet
the Title bestowed upon him, gives us a description of an Enemy,

0074.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bock of JOB. Verf.7.

body.t: or tells us more clearely what an Enemy is, or who is an Enemy.
He is an Enemy that risetb up against us; an Enemy riseth up in his
spirit against us, and he riseth up in his actions against us. He riseth
up to make us fall, he riseth up against us that he may rise above
us.
There are two sorts of Enemies.
First, Some are secret Enemies, that lye, possibly, in our very
bosomes, chat salute us courteously every day, as Judas did Christ,
with a kisse, and a haile Master, no appearance of an Enemy, ei¬
ther in words or actions; and yet, The detpest and most dangerous
Enemy, is the secret Enemy.
Secondly, There are open Enemies, professed Enemies, such
as hold out a flagg of defiance, and send challenges to us; such
one is here meant by these words; He that riseth up against me.
David (Psal. 41. 9.) describeth his Enemies by lifting up the
heele; He that did iat of my bread, lifted up bis betle against
me; that is, he hath acted opeuly against me, he hath kicked at
me like a wild horse, or would have trampled me under his feet.
To rise up,and to lift up the heele against one,are the same, as the
enemy in the Text, and he thit riseth up, are the same, and as the
wicked, and the unrighteous are the fame; only in these two last
different words, there is a different respect. Properly a man is said
to be wicked in reference to his Impieties against God; aud un¬
righteous in reference to his Injustice and wrong dealings with
man; Justice giveth every man his own, his due: and therefore
he who either by professed violenee, or secret fraud, opposeth an¬
other mans due, is unrighteous. Yet these words are often used
promiscuously, the wicked for the unrighteous, and the unrighte¬
ous for such another as the wicked; Let mine Enemy be as the
miched, and he that riseth up against me, as the unrighteous. In
these things there is no difficulty.
But though these words are plaine in their literall sence, yet
there is some difficulty in gathering up the meaning and Interpre¬
tation, as also the scope and designe of them.
Let mine Enemy be as the miched, may be Interpreted three
wayes.
First, As an argument of Tobs charity.
Secondly, As an argument of his piety.
Thirdly, As an argument of his courage and magninimity in

0075.head: Chap.27. An Exposition mpon ibe Book ef JOR. Vers.7

body.t: maintaining his own cause, still and stiffely insisting upon his In¬
tegrity; the sence is good, and the Interpretation faire cither ot
these wayes.
First, these words are expounded as an argument of Tobs cha¬
rity, ( Let mine Enemy be as the micked, and he that riseth up against
me, as the unrighteous) As if Job had spoken his mind thus; Te my
friends have adjudged me tobe a wicked mau, ye bave sentenced
me to be unrighteous: mell, let this be granted or supposed that I am
so, say (seeing ye have such a mind to it) that I am an uurighte¬
ous man, let me abide under this cloud of censure; all tbe hurt that
wish you, who are in appearance mine Enemies, and continually rise up
against me, is this, that ye mere such as Iam, whom ye call mic ked,
or that je were lihe him mhom ye sappose the uurighteous man,
would ye were as I am, except these sorrowes, except the bonds of
these sicknesses and sores, aud sore afflictions which are upon me; for
my partl mish that you mine Enemies mho dispute mith and oppose
me, wbo resist and rise up against me, were as my selfe, whom ye ac¬
count the wicked and unrighteous man.
Thus Paul (pleading his cause and Integrity before King A¬
grippa, and having almost perswaded him to be a Christian,Act:
26. 29. ) answered, I would to Gol that not only thou, but all that,
heare met his day, wtre both almost, and altogether such as I am,
except these bouds. As if he hid said, I am judged at an heritique
as a disturber of the peace, as a wicked man, I would that mine E¬
nemies and opposers were but as this heretique, as this seditious per¬
son, I would that thou O King, and all that hear me, were such as
am, except these bonds; I would beep my troubles to my selfe, and
mish tbat ye all were partakers of my grace and spiritual priviledges.
The exposition of Tobs wish now under hand, hath a paralel sence
with this of Paul. There is no greater argument of sincerity and
Gospel charity, than to be willing to beare the mhole of our own trou¬
bles, and that others should beare a part and share mith us in all our
mercies.
Secondly, The words may be expounded as an argument of
Jobs piety; and that tuo wayes.
First, Tob doth assert his piety, by ascertaining who or what
kind of men they were, with whom he had used to converse as
friends. As if he had said; Tou account me miched, and unrighte¬
ous, A man delighting in the society of the ungodly, doing them cour¬

0076.head: Chap.27. An Expositon npon the Boik of JOR. Verf.7.

body.t: tesies, and making them my Counsellers; mhereas indeed I have laok¬
ed upon the wicked and unrighteous as mine Enemies, even as tber
that rise up against me. It is an argument ot holinesse and piety,
to love those that are holy and righteous, to make them our
friends and favourites, who are friends to God, and the favourites
of Heaven. And to say of the wicked, he is my enemy, or let
mine enemy be as the wicked,is to act like a friend or servant of
God. When Tehoshaphat said to wicked Ahab, I am as thou art,
and my people as thy people, (2 Chron. 18. 3.) The Lord fenta
Prophet to him with this reproofe, Shouldest thou belpe the ungod¬
ly, and love them who hate the Lord? (2 Chron. 19. 3. ) Some are
kuowne to be wicked, by being companions of the wicked, and it
ill becomes those who are Godly to have any incimacy of com¬
munion with the wicked. And therefore Tob gives a probable
character of his own piety, by disowning ( according to this in¬
terpretation) the impious, and reckoning such in the number ot
his enemies.
Secondly, We may expound the words as an argument of his
piety, thus; As if Tob had said; Though I have spoken much about
tbe worlaly prosperity of the miched, jet I am so farre from judging
their Condition to be good, or their Estate happy, that I mould not
wish the worst Enemy I have in the world a worse lot than tobe
micked man; I could not desire any thing more evill to him than this,
that be were evill and unrighteous. And therefore you are much de¬
ceived in your judgment of me, as if mbile I have spoken of the pro¬
sperity of the micked, I were of opinion, that their Estate is good, or
they bappy; whereas indeed I looke upon them as men to be pittied,
not envied in the highest pitch of their worlaly pompe and greatnesse.
Andas I have no bunger after their danties my selfe, so I would
not wish any friend of mine to partake with them; but (were it law-
full to wish evill to an Enemy) I would not wist the vilest enemy
bave upon the sace of the earth a worse Condition, tban that of a wic¬
Rel man, hon much soever be flourifheth in the eye of the world.
Thus he seemes tobe of Moses his choyce Spirit, yes to hive
made his choyce like Moses (Heb. 11. 25.) Rather to suffer af¬
fliction mith the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for
seasen. This is a great argument of Tobs piety, shewing that he had
no desire, no suitablenesse at all in his spirit to the Condition of
wicked man, how glorious or glitrering so ever among men. It is

0077.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bock of JoB. Vers.7.

body.t: Common way of Expressing that vrhich we most distast, to say,
Let this be te mine Enemy, let this be to those that hate me. Aud
this supposeth such a displeasure against the person as cannot be
satisfied with any particular trouble. When Abigail came to meet
Dauid, and to interpose between him and her husbands destructi¬
on by his sword, she thus bespake him (1Sam. 25.26.) Nox
therefore my Lord, As the Lord liveth, and as tby soule livetb, See¬
ing the Lord hath withholden thee from coming ta shed blood, and
from avenging thy selfe mith thine onne hand, non let thine Enemies,
and they that seuke Evill to my Lord be as Nabal. Nabal was a pro¬
sperous man in the world, yet a wicked and a wretched man, and
the hand of God was upon him, and he dyed presently after; non
let the Enemies of my Lord (saith Abigail ) be as Nabal; that is,
let them be as vile and low in the esteem of men, as Nabal is, up¬
on whom one of his own servants could bestow no better lan¬
guage than Son of Belial, such a son of Belial, that a man could
not speak to (v. 17.) yea, let thine enemy be as unable to hurt
thee, as Nabalis, and let him as surely fall under the revenging
hand of God as Nabal shall, upon whom not to revenge thy selfe
with thine own hand, thou hast been so easily perswaded. We
have alike wish formed in the same termes (2 Sam. 18.32.)
The Ring said toCushai, is the young man Absolom safe? And Cu¬
shai said, let the Enemies of my Lord the King, and all that rise up
against thee be as that young man. When he would set forth the
miserable end and fall of Absolom ( who was hung on a tree and
slaine) he saith, let all that wish my Lord the King hurt, be ai that
young man is. Once more we read this way of imprecation,
Dan. 4.19.) Then Daniel ( whose name wis Belteshazzer
was astonied for an boure, and his thoughts troubled him: the King
spake and said, Belteshazzir, let not the Dreame, or the Interpretati¬
on thereof trouble thee; Belteshazzer answered and said, my Lord
the Dreame be to them that hate thee, and the Interpretation thereof
thine Enemies. Asif Daniel had said, I have cause enough to be
troubled, it is a black Dream, and the vision is a vision of darkuess
and astonishment; I could uish that thy Dreame were to thine
Enemies, and the accomplishment of it to them that hate thee.
In this language speakes Tob here; you think that I am a man
much taken with the prosperity of the wicked; for my part, Let
mine Enemies be as the miched, and they that rise up against me as

0078.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bock of JOR. Vers.7.

body.t: the unrighteous. That's the best esteem and highest value that
have of all them that are wicked and unrigheeous.
Hence Observe;
To be micked, or an anrighteous man, is to be in thi morst estate,
incident unto, or imaginable by man.
To be poore and despised, to be weake and sickly, all thefe e¬
vills of state, name, and body, are not evill at all, in comparison ot
sin. Morall evills are the worst of evills. And in the opinion ot
godly men, none are in so bad a condition as ungodly men; if it
were lawfull to wish the worst that could be to an enemy, the worst
we could wish him ( putting all evill wishes in one) is, that be
should be as the micked, and unrighteous. Indeed they who are like
them in wickedness, think none like them in happiness,and so they
think themselves. We have both these tempers, or distempers ra¬
ther, laid down in one verse ( Psal. 10. 3.) The mick ed boasteth
bis hearts desire(that is, when he hath gotten, which is not worth
the getting, what his heart desireth) and blesseth the covetous (that
is, counts them blessed) whom the Lord abhorreth. They who are
of the world, blesse the worldly, and blesse themselves in their
worldly blessedness, and would not turne Tables uith any in the
world unlesse such as have more ot the world than they, (P/.39.
2.) The wicked flattereth himselfe in bis omn eyes, till his Iniquities
found abominable. He thinks all is well with him, and so doe
many besides himselfe. Yea so ignorant, or impudent are some,
that they think God himselfe approves, and hath a good opinion
of the ungodly. Such bold blasphemers are at once discovered
and reproved by the Prophet, (Mal.2. 17.) Te have meuriad the
Lord nith your words, ret ye say wbtrein have me mearyed bim?
wben ye say every one that doth evill is good ( that is, approved, ac¬
cepted, and well esteemed) in the sight of the Lord, and he deligbt¬
etb in tbem, or wbere is the God of Jadgment? Which latter
vords are either a new accusation, ot the proofe of their former
accusation;as if they had said, if he did not delight in, and approve
them, he would punish them. This is ( as the Septuagint render)
provoking word, or (as the Chaldee hath it) a molesting trou¬
bling word; we render it fully, a wearying mord. Whit? when
God suffers wicked men to prosper and receive good, doth he ac¬
count them good? The Prophet Isaiah (Chip. 43.24.) presents

0079.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition apon the Book of JO2.

body.t: the Lord thus complaining; Thou hast wearied me with thine ini¬
quities. But that which wearieth the Lord most, is when man saith
ne is pleased with, or approves either iniquity wrought, or the
workers of iniquity. To speake or thinke thus of God, is not only
iniquity, but highest blasphemy. It is a most grosse error, when
man thinks so ot man, as the same Prophet shewes (Mal.3.15.)
And now ye call the proud happy; Such as are men of aspiring
minds, and work their own ends confidently, daringly, ye call
the ouly men. A proud man is the worst of wicked men; every
wicked man hath abundance of unmortified pride in him, but
pride is a predominant lust in some wicked men; how unhappy
and blind in judgment are they who call these happy? The pre¬
sent poynt saith, that all wicked men are in a bad condition, but
among them all, none is in so bad a one as the proud, for him God
resisteth (James 4. 6.) and if it must needs goe ill with chem,
nhom God doth only leave to themselves, not giving them assi¬
stance, then who can say how ill it must needs goe with them
(though never so high and great in the world) whom God re¬
sists, and sets himselfe against? There are two considerations,
which, shew how farre all wicked (much more proud)men are re¬
moved from happiness.
First, They are out of the favour of God, they have no roome
his heart. How miserable is their life, who share not in the lo¬
ving kindness of God, which is better than life? We enjoy no¬
thing that is truely good, without God, who is the cheifest good.
The light of his Countenance is better than all the comforts ot
this life: what have they that enjoy aot the light of his Counte¬
nance,but sorrow and darkeness? As it is the sm of a wicked man, so
is his punishment, that he is mithout God in the world. He is with¬
out God in the world, as to the feare of, or faith in his nime, this
his fin; and he is without God in the world, as to any favour
or good will which he bath from God, and this is his punish¬
cient. As whatsoever good a carnill man doth, whatever servics
he performes to God or for God, his heart, his good will is not
it; so whatsoever the wicked hive from God, they have none
ot his heart, nothing from his good will.
Secondly, Such are not onely out of the favour of God, but
(for there isno middle stite) they ire the subjects of his displei¬
sure, and stand naked to his wrath; they have no shelter, nothing

0080.head: Ctap. 27. Au Expositios upon the Bot et JOR. Verf.7.

body.t: to keepe off the dayly droppings, or most dreadfull stormes and
threatenings that are written in the booke of God. And indeed
there can be no shelter from divine wrath, but in divine love.
Therefore ( saith Tob) I would have no friend of mine, no childe
of mine, no neighbour of mine in such acondition as they are in;
Let mine Enemy be as the micked, and bim that riseth up against
me as the unrighteous. That’s a second Interpretation, represent¬
ing these words as an argument of Tobs piety, who, how much so¬
ever he had spoken of the prosperity of wicked men, yet was farre
from beleeving that any true happinesse belonged to them; the
choycest of their comforts, their most perfect prosperity, doth not
put them one step beyond misery.
Thirdly, We may Interpret these words as an argument of
Jobs Courage in his cause. And then, Let mine Entuy be as the
wicked, is either a Prophesie (mine Enemy shall be as the wicked)
or an Imprecation, I wish they were so. Miny read it onelyas
Prophesie (as was touch before ) foretelling uhat should become
of his Enemy. But what Enemy doth he meane? He meants not
Enemy in reference to his person, but to his cause; his enemy
was his opposite in judgment and opinion; and when he saith,
Let mine Enemy be as the micked, or mine enemy shall be as the
miched, he speakes ot their desert, not of his own desire, or he
speakesof what might justly befall them, not of what he would
have them fall into. As if he had said, mine enemy, or he that
opposeth me in this Cause, deserves to be as the wicked and to be
handled as the wicked, or in the carriage and handling of this
Cause mine enemy will be found as the wicked, and he that riseth
against me as the unrighteous. It is possible for a good man
engage in a bad matter, and in the uprightnesse of his own
heart to doe and say that which is not right. Holy Paul could say
ot himselfe before his conversion; I verily thought with my selfe,
that I ought to do many things contrary to tbe name of fesus of Na¬
zareth (Acts 26. 9.) And some after converfion have done things
contrary to the name and truth of Christ, how much more of theis
brethren. But no good man can oppose a good Cause, or a good man,
but he gets a staine upon bis goodnesse by it. It is Iniquity, or un¬
righteousnesse to vex any man in his righteous cause, or in the
righteousnesse of his cause. Tob speaks home and somewhat harsh¬
Iy, when he called his friends Enemies, but they had constrained
L

0081.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bok TJOE. Verf.7

body.t: him. Yet two things give some allay to the sharpness of his lan¬
guage.
First, That he did it onely inreference to the state of the bui¬
siness, not of their persons.
Secondly, That he did it to awaken, and stirre them up to con¬
sider what they had done. He speakes roughly to them, that they
might desist from speaking and dealing so roughly with him, and
forbeare to fasten the Censure of hypocrisie upon him. And we
find that the Lord himselfe in the close of this diipute, doth verifie
this Prophesie of Tob (Mine Enemy shall be as the micked) for the
Lord tells them (Chap. 42. 7.) when the business came before
him) My mrath is hindled against thee (namely Eliphaz) and a¬
gainst thy tro freinds, for ye have not spoken of me the thing that
right, as my servant Job. There God verified it, that Tobs ene¬
mies, or they that stood in this Cause against him were as the un¬
righteous, and wicked.
Secondly, We miy take notice of the qualification of this
speech, (Let mint enemy be as the micked, and he that riseth up a¬
gainst me as the unrighteous) he doth not positively affirme that
they who were Enemies to him in that cause or businesse, were
wicked, or were unrighteous, but let them be as the wicked,
While they take part and joyne with the wicked and unrighteous
in their Censures upon me, they make themselves such; such was
Jobs confidence in the goodness of his Cause, that he feared not to
affirme his opposers would be found as the unrighteous and the
wicked.
Hence, Observe;
He that opposeth a righteous Cause, acts the part of an unrighte¬
ous man.
I doe not say, ( por did Job) that every one that opposeth
righteous cause, is unrighteous; but he that opposeth a godly or
righteous man, in a righteous cau e, acts like an ungodly man, or
he takes up the worke or the unrighteous. Thus Tob said to his
wife (Chap. 2.10.) Thou speak est as mne of the foolish women use
speake; he doth not say. thou a.7 foole, or a xicked woman,
but in this thou actest like one oi them. Thus ? good man may
act as a wicked man, both in opposing that which is good, and in
complying with that which is evill, and so he may be numbred

0082.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bock of JOR. Vers.7.

body.t: with the wicked, yes deserve to be dealt with as the wicked, to be
wrapped upunder the same reproofes, and in the same Common
Calamities. We may quickly bring the rod of God upon our
selves, by being a rod upon the backes of others; and may sooner
or latter, feele hard blowes of correction from God, for the hard
words of Censure which our brethren have felt from us.
So then, when Job saith, Let mine Enemy be as the micked, he
doth not imprecate Evill upon his friends, because they apposed
him to have done so, had been sinful and dissonant to the rules of
charity; and it were as uncharitable for any to conceive he did so,
as for himselfe to have done it. And for proof that nothing of re¬
venge was upon his Spirit, he makes an open protestation to the
contrary accompanied with a secret and severe imprecation upon
himselfe, in case it were so (Chap. 31. 29.J. If I rejoyced at the
destruction of him that hated me, or lift up my selfe mben Evil found
him? Then &c. He that really wisheth Evilto his Enemy, cannot
but rejoyce when evill finds him. Joy ariseth from the accomplish¬
ment of desire. But though Tob did not wish evill to his friends,
yet he would not spare them in what they did ill, their ill dealing
with him.
Hence, Note;
It is no breach of Charity to speake home, and tell them mho op¬
pose the truth, that they doe wickedly, though otherwise they
be good men.
Truth is a friend to be preferred before all friends. We must
take heed of sowing pillowes under their armes, who maintaine
bad Cause; They who flatter and speake them faire, doe so. Such
lenitives encourage errour, and such gentlenesse is deadly to those
who ert. There is a sinfull provocation in sperking, especially in dis¬
puting;yet we may sperke plaine, & ell men their own, without any
just provocation. To maintain love & unity is good, but to main¬
taine purity is better. We must rather be against all men, than doe
any thing against the truth. Thus Paul dealt wich Peter ( Gal.2.
11.) I mithstood him to the face because he was to be blamed. His
holy zeal for God was not stopt by the respect and reverence
which he bare to man. Such wis Jobs courage according to this
interpretarion, while he said, Let mine enemy be as the micked.
can give no better Judgment of him in this case.

0083.head: Chap.27. An Expofition apon the Bok of JoR. Verf.3.

body.t: Vers. 8. For mbat is the bope of the bypocrite, tbough be bavs
gained, mhen God taketh amay bis soul?
Some conceive fob in these words giving a reason of what was
said before, that he had nothing to doe, in a way of compliance,
vith wicked men; for what is their hope when Gol taheth away
their soule? who would be in their coate, who though they flou¬
rish, and are gay while they live, yet will be most miserable when
they dye. Our reading seemes to carry this sence.
Further, We may expound this text as an argument by which
Job would prove that he was no hypocrite; As if he had said, Te
my friends bave long fince given your opinion of me, that I am an
hypocrite, and mere I indeed such a one, my Condition, I confesse, were
most miserable: although I might flatter my selfe mith the gain of out¬
ward comforts and advantages in this world, yet mhen I dye (it may
be to day before to morrow) I spould bave no true comfort in possession,
nor any solid ground to hope for it; For what is the bope of the bypo¬
crite, wbat comfort, or hope of comfort can he take up, when God ta¬
ketb away his soule? But if God take away my soule, I have bope;
amfully perswaded my hope shall not dye wben my body dyeth, there¬
fore I am no hypocrite, no wiched man. Tob hath given proofe in di¬
vers parts of this booke, that he had hope, and another spirit in
affliction than the wicked have, therefore his affliction did not
prove him wicked. First, he acknouledged all his afflictions to
come from God, yea from God as a father, while he wounded
him as an enemy. Secondly, in his deepest afflictions he begged
helpe of God. Thirdly, he hid hope of helpe, or would hope upon
God, though he should not help him; this no hypocrite ever did.
Yea Tob professeth, that though God should take away his soule,
yet he had hope, ( Chap. 13. 15.) Though he stay me, yet vill
trust in him; I will maintaine mine omn wayes before bim; be alse
my salvation, and an hypocrite shall not come before bim. Job could
trust God slay ing him, or taking away his soul, and therefore he
could not but have hope, if God should take away his soule. We
read ( Chap.6.8,9,1e.) that when he spake of dying, and of his
desire ro dye, yea, was begging that he might dye, he declared
lively hope, O that I might have my request, and that God would
grant me the thing that I long for; even that it would please God
destroy me, that he mould let loose his hand, and cut me off.

0084.head: Chap.27. An Expositon npon the Boitt ef JoR. Verf.8.

body.t: Thiu shall I yet have comfort: that is, that would be the most
comfortable newes to me, that I might but dye. This is my pro¬
fession, and this is my perswasion, I have hope in death, and there¬
fore I am no hypocrite, as you take me tobe; for wbat is the bope
ef the hypoerite, though he hath gained, mben God taketh amay bis
soule?
what is the bope of the bypocrite?
The meaning is the hypocrite hath no hope at all; he neither
hath, nor can have any hope when God taketh away his soule,
Hope is taken in Scripture divers wayes.
First, For the habit or grace of hope, implanted in the soule;
as there it a habit of faith, and a habit of love, so there is a habit
of hope, that is, an abiding principle of it.
Secondly, Hope is put for the putting forth, er for the acting
of this grace in our dependance upon God in greatest straits.
Thirdly, Hope is often put for the object of hope, and that
two wayes.
First, For the person in whom we hope. Thus God in Scrip¬
ture is ofren called hope ( Ter. 14. 8. )O the hope of Israel, &c.
That is, Othou, in whom thy people hope.
Secondly, Hope is put not onely for the person in whom we
hope,but for the thing or matter which we hope to attaine; the
good, the blessednesse which we look or hope for, is in Scrip¬
ture called hope, (Tit. 2. 15.) Looking for the blessed hope, and
the glorious! appearing of the Great God, and our Saviour Tesus
Christ. That blessed hope is, that state of blessedness which be¬
lecvers hope and waite for, at the appearing of our Lord Jesus
Christ. Here in this plice we may take in all, or any of these
sences ; Hypocrites pretend to the habit of hope, they seeme to
act hope, and to act it both upon God himselfe, and that blessed¬
nesse which sloweth out from him. But what is the hope of the hy¬
pocrite? it is nothing; He hath no hope in him, nor is any act of
hope put out byhim, either upon God, or upon the good things
which God hath promised in the world to come, how much soc¬
ver he hath gained in this morld. What is the hope of the hypocrite,
Though he hath gained.
There is a difference about the reading of this clause. Some

0085.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOB. Verf.8.

body.t: thus; That he should bring it about; So Master Broughton: Ihat
can be the hope of the hy pocrite, that he should bring it about; that is,
that he should perfect or make it good. The hypocrite may have
great hope (which really is only a great presumption) but he
cannot bring his hope about, he cannot compasse or obtaine that
which he lookes and longs for ?
Secondly, (reads another ) what is the hope of the hypocrite,
mhich he hath fulfilled, or brought abeut? As if he had said, The
hypocrite lookes but for morldly gaine, if he can fill bis purse, and get
preferment, if he can fill his belly and tabe his pleasure, he sits domne
satisfied, and saith, I have enough. Non what is the hope of the by¬
pocrite, though he hath fusfilled this hepe? though he hath gained
though he hath gottenas much at ever he expected? though he be as
rich or richer than ever he expected? though he be as great, and
greater, in this world, than ever he expected? though he have as much
pleasure and more than ever he expected ? what ii the hope of the hy¬
pocrite, though he hath fullfilled and reached the utmost line ofall these
hopes? may we not write emptinesse and inst fficiency, may we not
wiite mverknesse and uncertainty, may we not write vanity, yez
vexation of spirit upon the forehead of all these things? Then,
IVhat is the hope of the hypocrite, thoughhe hath gained?
Because the particular gaine of the hypocrite is not exprest in
the text, therefore we may affix any thing to it, that is gaine in
the esteeme of the world, or worldly men, as thus.
First, Though he have gained wife and children, that's one
gaine.
Second ly, Though he have gained credit, and a good name a¬
mong men, that’s another gaine,
Thirdly, Though he hath gained honour and au:hority above
men, though he be become a great man, one of the grestest men
the world, yes though he hath gained the command of the
whole world, what is his hope?
Fourthly, Though he hath been a Money-catcher (as a hei¬
then describes greedy Gripers ) like a Kite, or a Hawk, snatching
at all gaine as his game, avaritiously heuping up his prey, and glut¬
ting himselfe with, and glorying in his abundance, what is his
hope?
Fifthly, Though he hath gained ( which is a more precious
gaine than all thefe) all knowledg and learning in all Arts and

0086.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Verf.8.

body.t: Sciences, and be able to speike with the tongue of men and Au¬
gels, both to God in praying, and to men in discoursing and prea¬
ching, yet what is his hope,
When God taketh away his soule?
There are two readings of this last clause.
First, Some derive the word, which we translate, tabeth away,
from a roote, which signifies to be quiet, and to rest. Christ is cal-
led Shiloh from this roote, ( Gen. 49. 10.) The Scepter shall not
depart from Judah, nor a law-giver from betmeen his feet, untill
Shiloh come; that is, till Christ come, who giveth true rest, soule¬
rest, eternall rest to his people. And then the text is rendred thus;
what is the hope of the hypocrite, thougb he hath gained, and God
causeth his soule to rest, or to be quiet, and sit at ease in the use and
enjoyment of his gaine. This puts the best of the hypocrites case;
suppose that he hath gained much; suppose also that God gives
him a quiet possession of his gaine, which is not the lot of many.
Some get much, but their souls never rest, they are tumbled up
and downe with restlesse turmoiles in the world, they get much
trouble themselves, by what themselves have gotten. Thus So¬
lomon describes the condition of worldly gainers, (Eccl.2.22,23.)
What hath a man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his beart,
wherein he hath laboured under the Sunne? for all his dayes are sor¬
romes ( that is, he hath sorrow all his dayes) yea bis heart ta hetb
not rest in the night. And againe, (Chap. 5.12.) The abundance
of the rich will not suffer him to sleepe. Usually the things of the
world, either rest not with us, or make us rest-lesse; yet it must
be granted that some men gaine, and that greatly, and God cau¬
seth theit souls to rest, they are at esse in their possessions. Now
though this be the hypocrites present case, that after he hath
gained, God giveth his soul to rest. As the rich man advised his
soul (Luke. 12. 19.) Thou bast much goods laid up fer many
yeares, take thine ease, eate, drinke, and be merry. Suppose all this,
and let the hypocrites soul cake ease, lye downe and tumblein his
greatnesse, honour, and riches, let him rock himself asleepe in
carnal delights and delicacies, yet what is the hope of the hypo¬
crite, when he hath not on!y gained riches, bat gained ( which
better than riches) rest ? Though rest be good, yet the hypoc ires
rest is not good; His is a rest in sin, as well as in riches, and enat

0087.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition apon the Book of JOR. Verf.8.

body.t: not good; His is a false rest, and that is not good; His is a short
rest, a rest only fitting and fatting him for the slaughter, and such
rest is not good; though he hath rest, yet he hath no hope ot
rest, and what is hope in possession, where there is none in expecta¬
tion?
Secondly, Others derive the Original word from a root, which
signifies te pull away, to draw off, to draw eut; so we, mhat is the
hope of the hypocrite though he hatb gained, nhin God draws out,
er takes away bis soule; the soule is taken away by death, and that
by a naturall death as well as by a violent. But the word here used
doth properly imply a violent death, and that sence is most agrec¬
able to the present text, because the soul of a wicked man (as will
further appeare in the notes) is (as it were ) forced out of his bo¬
dy, though he dye (as we say) fairely upon his bed. The word
signifies properly, the drawing of a sword out of the sheath or
scabbard, which notion doth elegantly comply with that expressi¬
on of the prophet Daniel, who calleth or compareth the bedy of
man to a sheath; we translate him speaking thus of himselfe;
My Spirit was grieved within me ( Chip. 7. 15.) The Chaldee
is ( as we put in the Margin) in my sheath, that is, in my body:
the body being as the sheath, and the soule as the sword. When
God calleth the soule of any man out of his body, he unsheath’s
it. But he pulls the soule of a micked man out of his body, likea
rusty sword out of the sheath, which comes not out without much
strength and tugging. The word is also applyed to the pulling off
the shoo from the foot;our shooes doe not drop or fall off,but are
untyed & pulled off. Thus the word is used (Exod. 3. 5.) put off tby
shoois from off thy feet, for the place mhercon thou standest is boly
ground, saith the Lord to Moses when he appeared in the burning
Bush. The soule of a wicked man parts with his body like a strait
shoo, or a shoo fast tyed from the foot, very uncasily. So that un¬
der both allusions, the word implyes such a kinde of violence, in
the departure of the hypocrite out of this life, as if, loath to depart,
were alwayes his parting, his dying song. God putteth off, or pul¬
leth out the soule of the hypocrite, he doth not freely resigne or
yeeld it up when called to come forth. So much for the opening
of these words; what is the hope of the hypocrite, though he hath
gained, mhen God taketh away his soule. The Observations from
them are many.

0088.head: Chip.27. An Exposition apon the Bock of JOB. Vers.8.

body.t: First, A wicked man while he liveth may be fall of hope, and his
hope may live mith him as long as he liveth.
The hypocrites hope is nourished both with temporal and spi¬
ritual things. He hopeth that he hath the love and favour of
God, because he enjoyeth many outward (as he thinks) sa¬
vours from God. His estate is good here, and therefore he hopes
it will be so hereafter. Possibly he is rich, and great, and pro¬
sperous in the world, and thence concludeth, Surely God loves
me. Yea, and in reference to spirituils, the hypocrite may have
hope, he may be planted into Church-Priviledges, he may be
reckoned among Saints, or true believers; he may enjoy all the
Ordinances of the Gospel; he may eat bread at the Table of the
Lord, and sit among the Lords people; All which may breed
him a great deal of hope.
Further, He may have many and great spiritual gifts, yea,
may have a fair appearance of grace; As he often hath great
gifts of knowledge, of utterance, of prayer, so he may have that
which looks like grace, like faith, like repentance and godly sor¬
row, he may have that which looks like love and humility, and
patience, he may have the appearances of all these graces, and
these may wind up his hope very high, and fill his sayls with such
strong confidences, that he may reckon himself among the dar¬
lings of heaven, and the delight of Christ. He may look upon
himself, not only as in favour with God, but as one of Gods fa¬
vourites, and say in his heart, surely I shall be saved if any are to
be saved; he may come and lean upon the Lord, as the Prophet
tells us that sinful people did (Mic. 3.11.) The heads therefore
Tudge for reward, and the Priests thereof teach for bire, and the Pro¬
phets thereof divine for money, yet mill they leane upon the Lord, and
say, is not the Lord among us, nont evil can come upon us? But in¬
deed the Lord will do to him as another Prophet (Ezck.29.7.)
saith, Egypt did to the house of Israel, when they took hold of thee
by the hand, thou didst break and rent all their shoulder; and wben
they leaned upon thee thou brakest and madest all their loyns to be at
stand. Thus will the Lord do to all those who leane upon, and
make their boists of him, while their hearts are not perfect with
him. And therefore,
Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bock ef JOR.
Secondly, Observe;
Deatb puts an hypocrite quite off from all his hope; wben God
taketh amay his soul, bis hopeis also tak en away.
When he dyes, then all his hopes dye; as when the Princes of
the morld dye, their thoughts perish, so when they who are meer
worldlings perish, their hopes perish too. How can an hypocrite
hope for good in death, when his hope never enteted, nor ancho¬
red within the vail, for life? his hope is not fastened upon the
word of eternal life, and therefore his hope cannot be a stay to his
soul when he departs this life. The hope that holds out is entred
into that within the vail ( Heb. 6. 19.) that is, it closeth with
God himself in Jesus Christ, it hath sweet Communion with
God by Jesus Christ our high Priest, who as our forerunner is for
us entred into heaven. A beleever is subject to be tossed with
troubles of mind and manifold temptations, as a Ship upon the
Sea, while he is in this world; yet that hope which is entred
within the vaile, stayes him as an anchor sure and stedfast in all
stormes, and in all times. But the Anchor of the hypocrites hope
enters not within the vail, but is cast upon false and loose ground,
and therefore when the storme comes his anchor drives, and
unstedfast, and so his hope and heart fail together. The stoutest
hypocrite in the world will droop at last, when God comes to
take away his soul; then his crest falls, and his Plumes flagge.
When the rain descendeth, and the floods come, and the miuds blow,
and beat upon the house that is built upon the sand, it falls, and the
fall thereof is great (Math, 7, 27.) A false heart cannot hold out
in real hardships; when rain and floods and winds (by which are
meant all the troubles of this life) assault him, he runs to ruine,
and cannot stand his ground: much lesse will he be able to stand
in the hour of death, when the raine and floods and winds
temptations fall most furiously upon the soul. Thus Solomon con¬
cludes (Prov.11. 7.) wben a micked man dyeth, his expectation
shall perish, and the bope of unjust men perisheth. Possibly that may
be everlasting which they hope for, yet their hopes are not lasting,
the hopes of some perish, because they hope only for perishing
things; others have hopes of unperishing things, whose hope yer
shall perish. The voluptuous rich man is said to have had his good
things (Luke 16. 13.) he had no more to hope for, no more to

0090.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verf.8,

body.t: looke for, his hope perisheth when God tooke away his soule.
When a godly man dyeth, his hope is perfected by the fruition
ot that which he hoped for, he enjoyeth all and more than ever
he expected. But when an ungodly man dyeth,his hope perisheth
ina disappoyntment of fruition, he enjoyeth nothing at all of all
that, which he (though with little reason ) so much expected.
Againe, What is the hope of the hypocrite, though he bave gai¬
ned? The Spirit of God joynes gaine with the hypocrite.
Hence Observe, Thirdly;
Cruetousnesse and hypocrifie usually dwell together.
The true love of worldly gaine, and the false love of spirituall
çaine, hunt in couples, and are seldom severed. Hypocrisie aimes
at gaine, and often hits it, but it alwayes misseth true gaine;
falsenesse in the things of God, waites for fullness in the things of
men, but real fullness it gers none. When a false heart seeth that
religion is in credit, chat godlyness is the way to worldiy greatness
and that ( as sometimes it doth, though rarely) the profession of
leadeth to advancement, presently he takes upon him the pro¬
fession of Religion, and puts onthe garbe or fashion of godlynesse.
Christ saith of hypocrites, They devoure midomes houses, and for
pretence male long prayers. A false heart prayeth, and will be much
duty, that he may devoure the houses and estates of others,
or that he may smooth his way to his own ends; but he cares not
tobe, nor is he at all in duty to draw neare to God, or improve
his own spiritual estate to the end. This is a dangerous temptati¬
on in these times, because now religion is look'd upon with a good
eye, and religious godly menare in place; a false heart works up¬
on this, and will be in any forme of religion, that hath a faire ac¬
ceptance in the world, through the favourable eye of Princes and
earthly Powers, cast uponit. The Apostle speakes of some (ITim.
6.5.) who supposed that gain was godlyness; and surely the end
rhich such had in professing godlynesse, was that they might be
gainers, or have outward preferment by it. As for godlynesse in it
selfe, or abstract ly considered, they despised it, they cared no more
for it than for their old shooes; but the hope of gain was so sweet
to them, or they were so hungry and sharpe set after it, that they
counted godlynesse, which to their natural appetite was bitter,
or at best had no better tast in their palites, than the white of an
M 2

0091.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verf.8.

body.t: egge, tobe a pleasant morsel. Covetousnesse being predominant
the hypocrite, he will be so far a servant to any thing as it
brings in gain, which is the dyet and food of covetousnesse,
Fourthly, Job supposeth the hypocrite gaining.
Hence Note;
Hypocrites may, and usually do, gain much in this world,
As they have a great desire of worldly gain, so they get it;
they would fain have the world, and God saith, take it. The
Lord gives them (as he gave the Israelites in the Wildernesse,
(Psal.78.29,30.) their own desire, and they are not estranged from
their lusts, that is, they have what they will or lust to have, God
gives them their request (Psal. 106.15.) but sends leannesse into
their soul, yea, while the meat is in their mouths, the wrath of
God comes upon them. The hypocrite brings his hope about, he
fulfils his desire, and obtains what he projects; hypocrisie is to
some a very thriving trade. The hearts of Saints only are filled
with the hidden Manna, but the bellies of the wicked are often
filled with hidden Treasure (Psal. 19.14.) that is, with those
dainties and good things, which are vertually hidden in, and for¬
mally spring out of the belly and bowels of the earth. The Lord
casily grants them their wish in such things, and gives them theïr
portion ( which is all their portion) in this life. For as they are
but common professors, so these are but common mercies, such
as many of his Enemies receïve, who are but fatted as Oxen for
the slaughter, and fitted for destruction. True happinesse is not
tobe judg’d by lands or houses, by gold or silver. The world is
narrow bound : unlesse we get beyond the creature, and set our
hopes above this world, we cannot be happy. As hypocrites de¬
sire, so they attain much of the world, but they shall attain no
more, how much soever they seem to desire it.
Observe, Fisthly;
Riches or worldly gains avail nothing in the approaches
death.
The hypocrite (which Tob, Chap. 31. 24. professed he had
not done) maketh geld his hope, and saith to the fine gold, thou art
my confidence. But when pale death appears, when the King of
terrours sheus his face, neither gold nor fine gold can give any

0092.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bock of JOB. Vers,8.

body.t: comfort. The Apostle Paul could say upon a well-grounded assu¬
rance (Phil. 1. 21.) To me to dye is gaine. Happy are they who
gaine when they dye, but all the gains of this life cannot make us
dye happily. Solomon hath told us so, (Pro. 11.4.) Riches pro¬
fit not in the day of mrath, but righteousness delivereth from death.
Riches and profit are ( in common speech) the same things, yet
there’s a time whentiches are unprofitable. Many have been de¬
livered unto death for their righteousnesse (Math.5.10.)yet righ¬
teousness will deliver all that have it, from death; that is, from
the sting and wrath that is in death. But saith the Prophet (E¬
2ck.7.19.) Their silver and their gold shall not be able to deliver
them in the day of the mrath of the Lord, whether that be a day of
common publick destruction upon a Nation, or a day of particu¬
lar personil death. And seeing worldly things give us no reliefe
death, let not us linger after, much lesse live upon worldly
things; let not us live upon wvorldly things wnile we live here,
much lesse expect any thing from them when we go hence.
Godlinesse will stand by us when we dye, the riches of faith, the
gaine of spiritual knowledge and experience; the encreases of
grace which we have made, will stand by us, and stand us in stead
when we are dropping to the ground, and our frail bodies fal¬
ling into the Grave. When God takes away the soul of a belee¬
ver, all his soul gaines shall abide with him: But, mhat dotb all
that avail a rich man which he hath, if he hath not God, who gave
him all that he hath? They who (as Christ speaketh, Luke 12.20.)
lay ut treasure for themselves, and are not rich towards God, that
is, rich in the graces which they have received from God, and
rich in the duties and acts of grace which they have returned un¬
God. They (I say?) who are not thus rich towards God, shall
find no benefit sin all the treasures which they have laid up for
themselves,in the day of their greatest need, the day of death.
Sixthly, Job speaks here slightingly of all the hypocrites
gaine upon this account, because his soul continues in a lost con¬
dition. ivbat is the hope of the hypocrite though he hath gained,
Hence Note;
They are miserable who lose their souls, though they get much
of, or all this world.
He makes an ill market that puts off his soul at any price;

0093.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOR. Verf.8.

body.t: Christ, who knew the worth of a soul, and laid down a price to
the utmost worth of souls, puts these questions ( Math. 16.26.)
Mhat is a man profited if he shall gain the mhole worla, and lose his
own soul? or mhat shall a man give in exchange for his soul? that
is, he is not at all profited by all the profits of the world, if he
lose his soul; nor is there any thing in this world, which a min
giving, may receive his lost soul back again, as it were by way
of Barter and Exchange.
Secondly, From those words, When God tabeth away bis
soule,
Observe;
The soul is at Gods dispose, he may send for it nhen he will.
The Lord can command away the soul of the strongest, of the
richest, of the wisest ; Life and death are inthe hand of God. He
can either cut the thread of life, or spin it out at pleasure. Moses
tells the Jewes as one man ( Deut. 30.20.) He is thy life, and the
length of thy dayes. He also dispenceth death, and shortness of dayes.
The marriage of the soul and body together is life; the break¬
ing of this marriage bond, or the parting of soul and body
death. God can part the soul from the body, he can break that
marriage bond when & how he pleaseth. He can uncloath the soul,
and leave it naked, he can quickly stripit ot this garment of flesh,
The soul separate from the bodyis naked and uncloithed. So the
Apostle speaks about his own death (2 Cor. 5.2, 3, 4.) Not
tbat be mould be unc loathed, but eloathed upon, that mortality might
be swallowed up of life. When we are uncloathed or dye, mortali¬
ty swalloweth us up, but when we shall be cloathed upon with, or
live in glory, mortality shall be swallowed up. Now, as the time
when the body shall be cloathed with glory, and mortality shall be
for ever soalloued up; sothe time when the soul shall be uncloa¬
thed of this body, and this life swallowed up of mortality, is at the
appoyntment, and under the decree of God. When God will take
away the soul no man knows, only this we know, that he both
can and may take it away when he will.
Lastly, As these words (God tabeth away his soul ) imply
force,
Observe;

0094.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Bock of JoOR. Verf.8.

body.t: Though hypocrites and most micked men dye a natural death?
yet to them their death is violent.
Their souls are, as it were, snatcht and taken, yea rent and
torne from them, a wicked man doth not commend his soul into
the hands of God, but the hand of God taketh and pulleth his
soule from him. Old Simeon could say, Lord, non lettest thou tby
servant depart ix peace (Luke 2.29.) And Paul could say, I de¬
sire to depart (Phil. 1. 23.) No hypocrite could ever make any
of these prayers, for if his tongue hath spoken them,his heart hath
not. An hypocrite may somtimes desire to dye, but he is never
willing to dye. We read in the book of the Revelation (Chap.9.
6.) that many men shall seck death, and suall not find it, and spall
desire to dye, and death shall flee from them. But was this because
they were willing to dye?no, but because they were weary of their
lives, or afraid to live : they did not see any other good in death,
but to get out of the pænal evils of this life. Thus a wicked man
may desire to dye, that he may be quit of the troubles, miseries,
and dangers that threaten his life; but he is never willing to dye
when he quietly enjoys the good things of this life ; much lesse
doth he see that the best things of this lise are better’d in the next.
He doth not see that there is more good to come than any that
he leaves; yea, he will not leave his sin, his beloved lust, for any
good that is to come. And therefore though the Lord suffer him
to live till he be as fruit fully ripe, yea almost rotten, and ready
drop off the tree, though he be so old that he can live a natu¬
ral life no longer; yet his death is violent tohim. As the second
or eternal death rejoyns and reunites his soul to his body sore
against his will, so the first or temporal death separates and pulls
his soul from his body sote against his will. There are two spe¬
cial considerations, upon which it doth appeare, that a hypocrite
can never dye (in this sence) but a violent death.
Fisst, He cannot freely submit to the decree of death; he
cannot dye in obedierce as a true beleever doth. He that doth not
live in obedience, can never dye in obedience. As Christ mas obedi¬
ent anto death, eventhe death of the Crosse; So Saints (in their de¬
gree) are obedient, not only all their lives, but they are obedient
unto death, that is, their dying is an act of obedience. But it
impossible that the hypocrite, who never lived in obedience to

0095.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Verf.8.

body.t: the commandment of God, should dye in obedience to the de¬
cree of God,
Secondly, He hath no footing in, or assurance of a better
life; he never took hold of eternil life, therefore he can never
wiflingly let go his hold of a temporal life. No man willinglu
parts with what he hath, until he hath some evidence and assu¬
rance, at least some good hope of that which is better; or which
he (at least) conceives to be better than what he hath. A man
will not readily give up his possession of a smoaky Cottage, when
he sees,if he leave it,he must be exposed to all the injuries of wind
and weather, of frost and snow, in the open aire. So then, He
that hath not in him a principle of obedience, while he lives, nor
well-grounded hope of happiness when he dyeth, cannot dve wil¬
Iingly. And therefore, that is verified upon every wicked man
the world when he dyeth, which is said to the worldly rich map,
(Luke 12. 20.) This night shall thy soul be required of thee; His
soul is required, not refigned, tis taken away, not given up; and
though he say, he desireth to be dissolved, yet to be dissolved
none of his defire; He may choose death (according to his cor¬
rupt Judgment) as the lesser ever, but he never chooseth it
that which leadeth to the greatest good.
Thus we have seen somewhat of Jobs mind in asserting the
sincerity of his soul towards God, by his hope in God when his
soul should leave his body, while he in ’a way of diminution puts
the question, Ihat is the hope of the hypocrite, though he hath gai¬
ned, mhen God tabeth amay his soul?

0096.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Vers.9.

body.t: JOB, Chap. 27. vers. 9, 10.
Will God heare bis cry, mhen trouble cometh upon him?
Will he delight himself in theAlmighty? mill he alwares
call upon God?
N these two verses Job prosecutes and proves what he had as¬
serted in the former verse, that, The hypocrite hath no hope;
wbat is the bope of the bypocrite, when God taketb away bis soule?
He that hach hope shall be answered when he prayeth, God will
heare his cry. He that hath hope delighteth in Cod, when he
seeth nothing but causes of sorrow in the world. Hope encoura¬
geth the soule to secke unto God without ceasing inthe lowest
ebbe, and darkest night of outward trouble. But all these run
crosse to the hypocrite, He shall cry and not be heard, He hath
no delight in God, nor can he hold out long in calling upon God;
Therefore he hath no hope. Jobt proofe ariseth two wayes; He
argues, First, trom what God would not doe; Gol will not hear bis
cry, mhen trouble cometb upon bim, therefore he hath no hope,
that's his first argument; Second ly, He argues from what the hy¬
pocrite would not doe, and that in two particulars. First, his not
delighting in God; will be dolight bimselfe in the Almigbty?
The sence of the question is Negative; He will not, and therefore
he hath no hope. Secondly, He argues from his not persevering
prayer to God; will be alwayes call upon God? H: will uot,
and therefore he hath no hope.
Vers.9. wvill God beare his cry?
No; He uill not. The Lord heares thè least whisper of a gra¬
cious soule; the language of his heart, his thoughts, have a sound
in the eares of God; But the cry, the loudest cry of an' hypo¬
crite, God vill not beare, That is, he will not shew him favour
by granting him that which he cryed for. God hezres what
said in prayer, whosoever prayeth, but there are many prayers
made which he doth not grant; it is no good tous to be heard,
unlesse we be thus heard; in Scripture language, not to be helped
is not to be heard.

0097.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book ef JO2. Verf.9.

body.t: will God hear his cry?
By a cry we are to understand more than ordinary prayer,
crying is vehement praying; crying notes eartestnesse, or ferven¬
cy in prayer. This poore man cryed, saith the Prophet (Psal. 34.
6.) that is, he prayed mightily) and the Lord heard him, and saved
him out of all his troubles (Exod. 14. 15.) And the Lore laid
unto Moses, Wherefore cryest thou unto me ? that is, why dost thou
call so earnestly upon me? Moses cryed though he spake no¬
thing, it was the intention of his Spirit, nor the loudnesse of hĩt
voyce, it was the clamour ot his heart, not of his mouth that made
the cry. As in Scripture the multiplying of prayer, notes the in¬
tention of the Spirit in it (Isa. 1. 13.) w'hen you spread forth your
hands, I willhide mine eyes from you, yea, when you make many pray¬
ers, I will not heare; your bands are full of blood. So crying out
any on: prayer, shews utmost intention of the Spirit in it.
Will Gol heare his cry? That is, will he heare when he is most ur¬
gent and importunate in prayer? when his spirit is, as it were, all
on fire, or inflamed in prayer ? No, he will not ; God will not
only, not heare his floathfull prayers, and his sleepy prayers, his
cold-hearted, and dead-hearted prayers, but when he seemeth to
be most warme and lively in prayer, when he seemes tobe most
hearty and pressing in prayer, God will not heare him. This ag¬
gravates the misery of the hypocrite exceedingly; And yet that
which followeth, aggravates it much more, will Gol heare his
cry
when trouble comes upon him?
An hypoctite would not much care if he were not heard in times
of peace, & in the affluence of outward injoyments, but this pinch¬
eth him to purpose, that God will not heare his cry when trou¬
ble cometh upon him; such trouble as is a streïght, and puts him
between two walls, yea that puts him ( as it were) in the stocks,
or in prison, thit puts him in little ease; such a kind of trouble,
straightning trouble is here meant, yea and a vexing trouble.
Many troubles may come upon us, and yet not put us to streights,
we may be in trouble, and yet see our way out of trouble;but that
man is in a sad condition, who being in trouble knows not which
way to turne for helpe in the world, and while he turnes himselfe
God, God will not heare him.

0098.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOR. Verf.9.

body.t: uben trouble cometh.
The action or motion of a living creature is here ascribed to
trouble, treuble cometh; tis usuall in Scripture to speake so; and
is an allusion unto an adversary or an enemy, whether a single
person or an army. Thus it is expressed by Solomon ( Pro. 6. 11.)
So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an
armed man. The sloathsull man or sluggard ( for of him that text
speaks) sits still, but poverty is upon its speed, and travelleth
hard to over-take him; and as his poverty is said to come like
traveller, because it comes speedily, so it is said to come like an
armed man, because it comes violently, and as to him irresistably.
Thus trouble cometh upon the hypocrite, it cometh like an armed
mas, yea it cometh like a whole army of men, it incamps round
about him, and besieges him on every side. As Christ ipeaks of
Jerusalem (Luk. 19.43. )The dayes shall come upon thee, that
thine entmies shall cast a trench about thee, and compasse thee round,
and keep thee in on every side; they shall put thee, as it were, into
pound; That’s the Emphasis of the word, here trouble shall
come like an army of enemies upon the bypocrite, and then he
will cry aloud to the Lord for helpe, but the Lord will not heare
his cry. His troubles shall prevaïle upon him, and be remedilesse,
because his prayer doth not prevaile with God, but is returned
or sent bick anserlesse.
Hence, Observe;
First, Trouble shall come apon and overcome the hypocrite.
Many are the troubles of the righteous or upright, and the hy¬
pocrite doth not scape without his troubles; he meets them many
times in his way, and he meets them alwayes at his end. A godly
man may often meet with trouble in his way, but he never meets
at his end (Psal. 37. 37, 38. )Marke the perfect man, and be¬
bold the upright, for tbe end of that man is peace. But the trans¬
gressours fhall be destroyed together, the end of the xickel shall be cut
off; that is, either the thing which he proposed to himselfe as his
designe or end shall be cut off, or himselfe shall be cut off in the
end. An hypocrite must needs meet with trouble, because he
so sinfull, and when he meets with trouble, that must needs de¬
stroy him, because he lyes open, or naked to it, and hath no shel¬
N 2

0099.head: An Exposition upon the Book of Jo2. Verf.9.

body.t: Chap.27.
ter against it, he is not under the protection of God, he hath not
any one promise in the whole booke of God to friend, when ene¬
mies and troubles come. He is not fenced and fortified as the up¬
right are. God is a wall, even a wall of fire about his people,
he is their defence and bulwark, their strong tower and deliverer.
They have many fortifications against troubles; though they are
much assaulted, yet they ate well defended, God himself is their
fortification, their strong hold, they are not a naked people; but
an Hypocrite is exposed naked to the shock & shot of every trou¬
ble. Sin doth not only bereave us of our innocency, but ot our
safety. It doth not only closth us with impurity, but uncloath
us of power. When Aaron had made the Golden Calf, Moses
coming down from the Mount, both rebukes and questions him
about it; And he saw that the people mere nakel, for Aaron hal made
them nabed to their shame amongst tbeir entmies (Exod. 32.25.]
How had.Aaron made them naked?not by taking their cloaths off
from their bodyes; for he tooke nothing of them towards the
making of the Golden Calfe, but their Golden-earings (v.2,3.)
which they might well enough spare, and not be corporally na¬
ked: But Moses saw them stript of the protection and favourable
presence of God, which was not ouly as a garment to defend them
from cold and shame, but as an armour of proofe, or as a strong
tower to defend them from danger. A godly man sinning ren¬
ders himselfe sometimes thus naked; but a wicked man is alwayes
thus naked, he hath not a ragg of promise to put about him, and
therefore obnoxious to the incursions of every evill. His sin ha¬
stens the coming of trouble, and his sin leavs him unguarded when
trouble comes. He that dmelleth in the secret place of the most bip̨h,
shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty (Psal. 91.1.) and to
shew that a man resting in God is secure, be his dangers nevet so
great, & his cause never so desperate, the Psalmist gives assurance
to such a one (v. 4, 5. ) He shall cover thee mitb bis feathers
(as (which is Moses his allusion, Deut. 32.11.) the Eagle flutteritb
over her poung, or as (which is Christs allusion) tbe ben gat heretb
ber chickens under ber wings, so ] under his wing shalt thou trust:
his truth fhall be tby Sheild and Buckler, thou shalt not be afraid, for
the terrour by nigbt, nor for the arrow that flyetb by day. But the
hypocrites breast stands open like a Butt to all the the terrours and
arrows of the Almighty.

0100.head: Chap.27. An Expositon npon the Boett ef J0R. —Verf.9,

body.t: Now the troubles that come upon the hypocrite, are ot two
sorts; First, they are troubles from without; Secondly, troubles
from within, troubles of body and troubles of mind ; his consci¬
ence, which knowes what he hath done, and hath accused him for
what he hath done, is ready to vex and trouble him for what
he hath done. Conscience having judged and condemned him,
wounds and torments him, and he hith nothing either to keepe
off the stroik otit, or to heale it. Thus all sorts of trouble in¬
vade and assault him, while he hath no reall remedy or releife a¬
gainst any of them. For God mill not heare his cry when trouble
cometh upmn him.
Secondly, When Job querieth, Wil God heare his ery, &c.
he supposetn and tikes it for granted, that he will cry, when trou¬
ble comes upon him.
Hence observe;
Even hypocrites mill pray in times of trouble.
They have the form ot prayer, who neither have any power
with God in prayer, nor have ever felt the power of it upon their
own hearts. Heathens who know not the true God, have been
kuowne to pray, and will pray in trouble, then much more will
hypocrites, who both know and professe his name. It is natu¬
rall to pray in trouble, and therefore no marvaile if they who
have no grice fall on their kuees, and cry out for mercy, when mi¬
sery falls upon them. God is neer in the mouths of many (as the
Prophet expresseth them, Jer. 12.2.) yet farre from their reines.
They greatly desire helpe from him, though they doe not at ill
desire him. The prophet (Isa. 16.1 2. ) saith ot Idolatrous Moab,
It shall come to passe, tbat wben it is seen, that Moab is meary ou the
biph place, that he shall come to bis sanctuary to pray; that is, when
he hath laboured in vaine, by offering Sacrifices in the high place
other Idois for protection, then he shall apply himselfe by prayer
to Cbemosh his cheif Idol God, in that prophane Sanctuary built &
dedicated to that dunghill deity, as his last refuge, yet still in vaine.
And we read that when the storme was up, those Marriners being
afraid, Cryed every man unte his God, (Jon: I. 5.) These Marri¬
ners were Heathens and sived without God in the world, yet eve¬
ry one of them had his God. It is naturall to own a Ged, but to own
the one God is a work of Grace. And natural men who seldom call

0101.head: Chap. 27. Au Expofition upon the Bok of JOR. Verf.9.

body.t: upon God, and are therefore by the Prophet (Ter. 10. 25.) cal¬
led the familyes that call not apon bis Name, and by the Psalmist,
such as have not God in all their thoughts, ( Plal.10.4.) that is,
God is not at all in their thoughts; yet these will go to God and
call upon him; when they are so urged with stormes, that they
know not whither else to goe, nor any beside to call upon. Yea,
they who know God and professe his nime, are somtimes negli¬
gent and remisse in prayer, till they are quickned by their own
smart, (Isa. 26. 16.) Lord, in trouble bave they visited thet, they
powred out a prayer mhen thy chastening mas upon them. Grace act¬
ed little in that people till sence was touched; afflictions quickued
them to duty, and the rod of God upon their backs, was a memnes
to stirre theit hearts to God. Before they prayed as if they did
not pray, then they prayed as if they did nothing but pray, or had
nothing to doe but to pray. Lord, in trouble bave they vifited thee.
God had little of their company, few of their visits, till he visited
them; he had scarce drops of prayer, when they had showres ot
mercy. But when the Lords chastning hand was upon them, they
powred out showers of prayer. Nowas trouble occasions a god¬
Iy man to pray much, and the straites which God sendeth him, send
him to God with a more enlarged heart; so trouble vill compell
them to pray, who seldome use to pray at all, and never delight at
all to pray. When nature suffers, meere natural men will cryto
God, the grosse hypocrite willt hen call upon God, much more
the refined, or fine spun hypocrite; They who never made God
their choyce, will sometimes make bim their refuge.
Thirdly, Observe;
A micked man will not only pray in trouble, bat be mill prar
carnestly.
His prayer may amount to a cry. When Moses was in that
great streight, he did no more as to the outward act, he did but
cry to the Lord. Hypocrites will doe sotoo (1 Kingi 18. 28.)
It is said of Baals Priests that they cryed; They cryed loud, and cut
themselves after their manner mith knives and lanchers, till the
blood gushed out upon them; see, how vehement they were in
their superstitious de votien, they cryed, O Baal, beare us, they ery¬
from morning untill noone; an hypocrite will doe all that
godly man doth, as to the outside ofit, he will pray and pray a¬

0102.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bek of JOR. Verl.9.

body.t: loud, he will cry and cry aloud; so farre as prayer is a bodily ex¬
ercise he will goe; yea, so farre as prayer is an exercise of the soule
with respect to bodily or selfish ends,he will goe too, & that with
earnestness. Want of outuard good,and feare of evill, will make
the worst of men bestirre themselves. The Prophet brings in the
Lord at once discovering and disowning such importunate suiters
for their bellies ( Hos. 7. 14.) They cryed and they howled,
but (saith the Lord) They havefniot cryed uuto me mith their heart
wben they howled upon their beds; with what then did they cry and
howle, if not with their hearts? the same verse resolves us, that
they cryed with their bellyes, for it followes, they assembled them¬
selves for corne and for vine, and they rebel against me. Here’sthe
true Character of a hypocrite; first, He secks God for the loives;
secondly, he prayetb, and sinneth, he secketh the favour of God,
but rebels against the will of God; thus he runs his round of pray¬
ing and secking, of sinning and rebelling; he may be very earnest
the two former, but is most earnest in the latter.
Fourthly, Note;
It is trouble chiefty, if not only, which moves a hypocrite to pray.
A day of trouble is not only the speciall time when an hypo¬
crite prayeth, but it is, upon the matter, the only time. Trouble
that speciall time wherein a godly man prayeth; is any one af¬
flicted ? let him pray ( James 5. 13.) yet he prayes at all times;he
prays not only because he hath need to pray, but because he loves
to pray, and finds sweetness i the act as well as inthe answer or
issue. But a carnall heart hath no mind to the duty, but when he
goaded on by trouble, or driven by necessity; and then his mind
more upon the supply of his necessity than upon the right and
holy performance of the duty. A good heart prayeth in trouble,
but when trouble only mabes us pray, that is an argument of an evill
beart (Psal. 32.6.) For this shall every one that is godly pray unte
thee, in a time when thou mayest be found, or, in a finding time.
But what meanes the Psalmist when he saith, For this shall every
ons that is golly pray unto thee? What is this, For this? I answer,
It may referre either to the mercy already shewed him in the for¬
giveness of his sin, mentioned in the former verse, or to his pro¬
tection in, and deliverance from danger, promised in the latter end
of this; For this, shall every one that is godly pray unto thet, in

0103.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition apon the Bok of Jo2. Veff.3,

body.t: time mhen thou mayest be found: Surely in the floods of great maters
they shall not come nigh anto him; that is, these sloods shall not,
these floods of great waters are great afflictions and tribulations.
which is a frequent allusion in Scripture (Psal. 69. 2.) L am come
into deepe waters ( of trouble) mhere the floods (of sorrow and tri¬
bulation ) overflow me, and againe (v. 15.) Let net the water¬
floods (thit is, violent afflictions ) overflom me. When these floods
of great waters are up and threaten to sweepe us away, then is
time, wherein the Godly man pow:s out floods of prayers and
teares to God sor helpe; But the springs and streams of prayer
are not dryed up in him in the fairest day and warmest Sunshine
of outward peace and prosperity. He prayeth in sicknesse, and so
he doth in health; he prayeth inpoverty, and so he doth in ri¬
ches; He prayeth in a time of darknesse, and so he doth when the
candle of God shineth upon his head, and he washet h his foot¬
steps with butter. He secks releife by prayer in bad times, and
prayer is a refreshing to him in the best times. As for the hypo¬
crite, till trouble is upon him, God' heareth not of him, he doth
not pray that he may doe an honour to God, and shew his love to
God, or because he re joyceth in communion with God, but be¬
cause he would get off his burthen, and be at ease, for this he
prayeth, and prayeth hard. Pharaoh prayed, and he begged o¬
thers to pray for him when he was in trouble, (Exod. 8.8.) Then
Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron, and said, Intreat the Lord,
that he may take away the frogs from mi, and from my people, and
will let the people got, that they may do sacrifice unto the Lord.
take away the frogs from me, they troubled him; but he said
not, O take away my hard heart from me; that troubled him
not. And againe we have him in the same tune, (Chap. 10.17.
Non therefore forgive, I pray thet, my sin only this once, and intreat
the Lord your God, that he may take away fron me this deatb enty.
this death; Himself prayed, and besought Moses to pray also;
but, what was it for? what moved him to pray? It was, that death
might be removed, not sin, or if he prayed that sin might be re¬
moved, it was only as to the punishment of it, not as to the pollu¬
tion ot it. When Peter spake those bitter words to Simon Ma¬
gus, telling him he was in the Gall of bitternesse, (Acts 8 24.) Then
Simon answered and said, pray ye to the Lord for me, that none
these things wbich ye have spoten, come upor me. He did not begge

0104.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bock of JOB. Vers.9.

body.t: their prayers thit he might be delivered from his sinfull state,
from the gall of bitterness, and the bond of iniquity, in which Peter
told him he then was, but that he might be deliver ed from thit
miserable state in which he feared shortly to be; pray that nore of.
these things which ye have spoken come upon me. The heart of the
hypocrite is cheifely drawne out to prayer in two cases: Fisst, 10
prevent trouble threatned, as Simon Magus, O pray that none ot
these things may come upon me; Secondly, to get off, or eut of
trouble inflicted, as Pharoah, O pray that these froggs, this death
may be taken away. We must pray, and that earnestly, when
trouble cometh, but we must not deferre prayer, no nor earnest
prayer till trouble cometh. A godly man lookes upon trouble as
the occasion ol prayer, but the hypocrite, as the cause of it.
Fifthly, Observe;
God doth not regard nor ansmer the prayer of an hypocrite, no not
in trouble.
As wicked men do every thing igainst the godly, so every thing
with God, but prevaile. They may prayas facob did in his trou¬
bles, but they fhall not be Israels, Princes & prevailers with God
prayer as Tacob was. God vill not heare their cry when trouble
cometh, though they come to him in trouble. But some may say,
how then doth the Lord answer his own promise? (Psal. 50.15.)
Call upon me in the day of trouble, I mill deliver thee, and thou shalt
glorifie me. And againe (Isa. 65. 24.) Before they call I will an¬
smer, and while they are yet speaking I will heare. If the Lord hath
promised to heare before we call, will he not heare when we call?
answer; God is true to his own promise of hearing prayer, but
he never promised to heare the prayer of the hypocrite. He hath
promised to heare prayer; But first, it is the prayer of the upright,
Pro. 15.8.) The Sacrifice of the mich ed is an abomination to the
Lord, but the prayer of the upright is his delight. The blind man
could say, Now we know that God heareth not sinners: but if any
man be a worshipper of God, and doth his will, him he heareth,
(To. 9. 31.) But some may say, doth not God heare sinners?
why, whom doth he heite then ? if he heare not sinners, he, must
heare none; for all are sinpers. I answer; God heareth not sin¬
ners, that is, such as deligne in sin, and live in a state of sin, espe¬
cially when such pretend highly to holiness and the ways of God,

0105.head: An Exposition apon the Bok of JOR. Verf.9.

body.t: Chap. 27.
as most hypocrites doe. All persons unregenerate are sinners in
the sence of that Scripture, and so God may be said, not to heare
any of them, but hypocrites are the worst of sinners,[for they not
only have sin in them, and are in sin, but live in sin, and love their
sin, while they pretend love unto God. While they pray, they re¬
gard iniquity in their heart; and of such David saith, God will
not hear their prayer;yea he puts the case,not in a second or third,
but in his own person, (Psal. 66. 18.)If I regard iniquity in
my beart, the Lord mill not heare me. It is possible for a godly man,
David, under temptation, to shew so much countenance to this
or that iniquicy, as may justly be interpreted a regarding of it in
his heart; and when he doth so, even he may have his prayer re¬
turn’d with a present slight instead of a grant ; yet I conceive that
supposition is rather put to shew the certainty of the thing, that
God will not heare the prayer of such as regard iniquity in their
hearts, than to shew that David or any godly man may regard
iniquity in his heart. As when he saith ( Psal. 46. 2.) me will not
feare, though the tarth be removed; It doth not suppose, the remo¬
ving of the earth, but is a strong proofe, they should not feare;
So when David saith, It I regard iniquity in my beart, tbe Lord
will not heare me. The supposition doth only give a stronger
proofe, that God will not hear their prayers, who regard ini¬
quity in their hearts. And to doe so is the very spirit of hypo¬
crisie. The hypocrite evet regards iniquity in his heart, what pro¬
fessions soever he may make, or how bitterly soever he may
speake against it with his mouth; though he complaine against
sin, yet he complyeth with it; though he disclaime it in words,
yet his soule cleaveth to and closeth with it, therefore God will
not heare his prayer. The Lord hath not promised to be nigh un¬
them in the things they call upon him for, whose hearts are
farre from him, and false to him in the things which he commands
and requireth of them. The promise runs in this tenour; The Lord
