nigh to all that call upon him, to all that call apon himin truth,
(Psal. 145. 18.) And thit a twoiold truth; First, ccording to
the truth of his rule; Secondly, in the truth of their own hearts.
The latter part of the verse is a correction of, or gives direction
about the former; As if the Psalmist had said, when I say, the
Lord is nigh to all that call upon him, my meaning is, he is nigh,
not to all that call upon him any how, or in any manner, but to

0106.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Rook of JOR. Verf.9.

body.t: all that call upon him in truth; and indeed others doe not, truly,
call upon God at all. Secondly, the Lord hath promised to heare
prayer, but whose prayer? the prayer of a beleever; now an hy¬
pocrite hath no faith; he hath much presumption, but no faith;
it is an easie mitter to beleeve, besides the promise, or withouta
promise, (as every hypocrite doth) but it is a hard matter to be¬
leeve upon, or in the promise. And the Apostle concludes,
(Heb. 11. 6. ) thit without Faith it is impossible to please God, for
be that cometh to God (in prayer ) must beleeve, that God is, and
that he is a rewarder of all them that diligently seeke him. Wbat¬
soever ye shall ask in prayer beleeving ( saith Christ, Math.21.22.)
ye shall receive; aud his meaning is, that without beleeving, we
shall receive nothing. They who pray beleeving, aske according
the will of God, both for matter aud manner, and are there¬
fore heard: But they who pray presuming, iske contrary to the
will of God, either for the matter or the manner, and therefore
are not heard. Thirdly, God hath promised to heare prayer, but
whose prayer? the prayer of the humble, of the broken-hearted,
and contrite, ( Psal. 51.17.) He that hath not faith, hath nothing
to get a mercy with, and he that hath not a broken heart, hath
nothing to put a mercy in. Now the hypocrites heart is a proud
and an unbroken heart, therefore his prayer is not under a promise
be heard. Fourthly, the Lord promiseth to heare prayer, but
whose prayer? it is the prayer ôf a willing people, or of such
whose prayer is a free-will-offering. David prayeth (Psal. 119.
108.) Accept I beseech thee, the free-will-offerings of my mouth;
that is, those supplications which my mouth freely offers. But the
hypocrites prayer is not a free-will-offering, he prays not because
he is free to the duty of prayer, but because he would be freed
from trouble by prayer. He prayes only ro have his turne ser¬
ved, or to get an almes. Now that prayer which is not a free¬
will-offering, is not accepted of the Lord. From the induction of
these particulars (and many more might be added ) it appears
that the hypocrites prayer is unheard, and unanswered, not be¬
cause God doth in the least forget or fayle in his promise of hear¬
ing prayer, but because the hypocrites prayer comes not into the
account and qualification of those prayers which God hath pro¬
mised to heare and answer. God only heares the prayer of the up¬
right, of the beleeving, of the broken-hearted, of the willing, the
O 2

0107.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book ef J0R. Vers.9.

body.t: ypocrites prayer is none of these, and therefore is not undera
promise to be heard. Yea the Scripture thunders agaïnst him,
when he seemes to thunder to heaven in prayer: David speakes
thus (Psal. 18.40,41.) Thou hast given me the neches of mine
enemies, that I might destroy them that hate me; They cryed, but
there was none to save them; and least we should think they cry¬
ed to false gods, or knockt at a wrong doore for helpe, he adds,
They cryed, even to the Lord, but he ansmered them not, and what
followes? Then did I beat them small as the dust before the minde:
did cast them out as the dirt in the streets, that is, notwithstanding
all their crying and praying for favour, the Lord declared his high¬
est displeasure against them, and gave them no answer, but by gi¬
ving them over to destruction. Further, the Lord is so far from ac¬
cepting such prayers, that he hath cast them not only as sinfull
but as fin; then he shall be judged, let him be condemned: and let
bis prayer become sin, ( Psal. 109. 7.) The prayer of the hypocrite
sin formally, and it is sin in the effect, that is, in stead of get¬
ting any good by it, he gets hurt, and the Lord instead of helping
him because he prayeth,punisheth him because of the sinfulness of
his prayers. Thus his prayers become sin to him, because he re¬
ceives no more respect from God when he prayes, then when he
sins. And sin doth not only mingle with his prayer (as it doth
with the prayers of the holyest ) but his prayer is nothing else but
mixture er mingle mangle (is we speak) of many sius. The
Spirit in wonderfull straines of holy Eloquence prosecutes this
poynt against hypocrites (Pro. 1. 27, 28.) When your feart com¬
eth as desolation, and rour destruction cometh as a mhirl-wind;
when distresse and anguish cometh upon you: then shall they call up¬
me, but I will not answer; they shall secke me carly, but they
shall not find me: for that they hated knowledg, and did not choose
the feare of the Lord. Here’s calling without answering, and early
seeking without finding. And hath not the Lord reason to take
no knowledg of them calling, who hated the knowledg of him
commanding, and not to deliver them from their feires, who did
not chuse his feare? Is it not just, that when God call to duty,
and man will not answer by obeying him, that man should call in
misery, and God not answer by releeving him ? Againe (Isai.
15.) Wben you spread forth your hands, I mill hide uine tyes from
rou; yea, mhen you mabe many prayers I will not beare: your bands

0108.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Vers.9.

body.t: are full of blood. (Ter. 14.12.) Ivhen they fast I will not heare their
cry (Ezek.8.18.) Though they cry in mine cares mitb a loud voyce,
jet nill I not heare them. Once more, (Mic. 2.4.) Then shall
they cry unto the Lord, and he will not ansmer them, he will even
hide bis face from them at that time, as they have behaved themselus
in their doings. Thus in Scripture all along we find nothinz
but Negatives and denialls upon the prayer of the wicked; They
who behave themselves ill in their doings, do in vaine aske or ex¬
spect good from God in the time of their sufferings. The effectual
fervent prayer of a righteous man avayleth much (James 5. 16.)
But how fervent soever the prayer of a wicked manis,it is neither
effectuall nor avayling. A hypocrite may morke hard in prayer,
but bis prayer workes not.
Sixthly, The design of the whole verse, being to shew the
miserable condition of an hypocrite upon this single account, be¬
cause God will not heare him in his misery. will God hear his cry
mhen trouble comes upon him?
Observe;
Not to havt prayers beard in treuble, is the worst of all
troublis,
It is worie than all the evills that take hold of us, that our
prayers for the removing of evil are rejected. This is the worst
of a wicked mans bad estate, the Lord will not heare him when he
cryes. And this is the best of the Saints good estate, that the Lord
ready to heare their cry. That which Moses spake, as the pri¬
viledg and happinesse of the Jewish Nation in generall, is true
of every true Israclite in particular, (Diut. 4.7.) What Nation
there so great, who hath God so nigh unto them, as the Lord our
God is, in all things that me call upon him for? this was a peculiar
mercy to them above all Nations, that God was nigh unto them
all things that they called unto him for; and this is the happi¬
nesse of every true Israelite, of every Jew in the Spirit, God
nigh unto him in all the things that he cryeth unto him for; and
God is thennearest to him when trouble is nigh at hand.It sets the
heart above all dangers, yea it makes our very dangers a safetyto
us, to have an assurance that God uill be with us, in danger, for
the asking. So the Apostle (1 Job. 5. 14.) This is our confidence
that ne haut in bim, (that if me ast anp thing according te his mill
Chap. 27. An Exposition apon the Book of IO*.
he hearetb us. This is the confidence of Saints in a double noti¬
on. First, it is their confidence, or they are as confident as confi¬
dence it selfe, that God will heare them in trouble; Secondly, that
God will heare them mikes them as confident as confidence
selfe in the midst of troubles. “Tis reckoned a happinesse among
men (and the confidence of man riseth high upon it) to have the
care ot Princes, that whatever we ask we shall be heard in it by
those in power. To have audience and acceptance with Great men
a great priviledg among men; no man can tell what he hath got,
when he hath gotten a great Kings eare; how much more is this
true, when we hàve got the eare o! God, who is the King of Kings.
Davids great desire was (Ps.19.14.) Let the words of my moutb, &
meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sigbt, OLord my strengtb
and myredeemer. When those words of our mouths which flowt
from the meditation of our hearts are acceptable in the sight
God, what can we want, while we have an heart to meditate upon
the fullness of God, or a mouth to expresse our owne wants? If
man had all that in his hand which this world could afford him,
and God should say, I will not heare thee, his all were nothing:
he had riches and honour and pleasure, if he were a petty god
upon the earth, yet if he cannot be heard in heaven, he may say as
Haman (after the boist of all his Greatuesse ar Court, and riches
home) because Mordecai the Jew sate in the Kings gate, and
would not bow to him, what doth all this availe him? The mea¬
nest and most afflicted beleever is better than he, because God
heareth him. We may quickly see the outside, the end of all per¬
fection, (Plal. 119. 96.) that is, of all worldly perfection. But
who kuowes what this may produce and bring forth, that God
doth hear us and accept us, and is ready when we come with peti¬
tions to give an answer. As the Spirit ot prayer is the most ex¬
cellent gift, so the hearing of Prayer is the most comfortable gift.
Though me lye among the pots, yet if God hear us, all’s well, then
shall me be as the wings of a Dove covered mith silver, and her fea¬
thers with yellow gold, (Psal. 68.13.) Holy desires and prayers are
thewings of the soule by which we mount ( as doves ) aud ascend
spirit unto God; and if the Lord heare and grant those desires
and prayers, then our wings are indeed silver’d and gilded over,
richly laden with blessings and with mercyes. Will God hear our
ery in trouble? is at best a heart-troubling word. God mill heare our

0110.head: Chip.27. An Expositon npon the Bock of JOR. Vers.10.

body.t: cry in trouble, is a heart-reviving and quickning word. God will not
biare our cry in troubli, is a beart-breaking, a killing word; and
that's the hypocrites mord. Will God heare his cry, when trouble com¬
eth upon him? He will not.
We have seen in this oth verse, what God will not do for the
hypocrite; now we shall see what the hypocrite will not doe in
reference to God.
Verf. 10. Will be deligbt himselfe in the Almighty? will be al¬
mayes call apon God ?
He vill cry unto God, but will he delight himselse in God:
he will cry unto God sometimes, but wils he alwayes call upon
God? He may be violent in duty, but he is not constant. Thus
the hypocrite failes and falls short.
will he delight himself in the almigbty?
The word here translated to delight, as also whit it is to delight
our selves in any person or thing, was opened at the zóth verse of
the 22d Chapter of this booke, and therefore I passe it here.
Mr. Broughton teads the text thus, and so doe some others, not
will he, But can he delight bimself in the Almigbty? As if the
sence were, it is a thing impossible that he should. To delight in
God is one of the highest exercises of Grace, and how can he doe
that, who hath no grace at all ? The hypocrite cannot find com¬
fort in God, when the world affords him none, as a Godly man
can.
We render well, mill he delight himselfe in the Almigbiy?
As if he had said, As the Almighty will not grant his request, nor
give him in his delight, that is, the thing which he desired, so he
hath no will, no mind at all to delight in the Almighty. The pro¬
per matter of delight is to have what we desire, and to enjoy what
we have. The hypocrite hath no pure desire to have or enjoy
God, but his desire is to have aud enjoy somewhat from God,
and when once he perceives that he cannot obtain that from God
which he delights in, he hath no delight at all in God. Desire is
love in motion, and delight is love at rest. The hypocrites will
doth not rest in God, but runs out many wayes after creatures;
after them he will goe, and therefore he hath no will to delight in
God, which is to rest in God, when God denies him the creature,

0111.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOB. Vers.10.

body.t: which he so much desired to rest in, as will appeare surther m the
Observations. Only, before I come at them, we may take notice
of the Title by which God is here expressed, as not delighted in
by the hypocrite. Will he delight himselfe
In the Almighty : or, upon the Almighty?
This name of God Shaddai, imports both his power and his
goodnesse. God is a full store-houle, or a most plentifull Spring of
all good to his People, ready to conveigh and give out himselfe
for tue supply of all their needs. He is, and hath everything which
may draw out desire, and render him(as was said of Titus Vespati¬
an, but it is infinitely more true of God) The delights of Mangind,
yet there are but few among the sons of men, whose desires and
delights meet and center in God. And such is the falseness of the
bepocrites heart, that though he seeme to make much love to
God, yet this Negitive interrogation is true ot him; Will he de¬
light himselfein the Almighty?
Hence, Observe;
First, They who are godly delight in God.
Yea they delight in nothing but God, or that which carrieth
the appearance, or beares the image and impression of God upon
it. Thus they delight in the word of God, in the work; of God,
whether of creation or providence, in the wayes and ordininces
of God, in the servants and people of God, in mbom David (as
type of Christ) said (Psal. 16. 2.) is all my delight; and all be¬
cause in these persons and in these things the invisible things
God, his power and wisdome, his holiness and goodness are seene
and as it were, made visible. While Moses calls the people of Is¬
rael to delight in the good things of God, he teacheth them to
terminite all their delight in the Lord himselfe, (Deut. 12.7th
18th verses compared.) And there ye spall eat before the Lord your
God, and ye shall rejoyce in all that you put your hands unto, ye and
your housholds, herein the Lord thy God hath blessed thee. But thou
must eat them before the Lord thy God, in the place which the Lord
thy God shall choose, thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy
man-servant, and thy maid-servant, and the Levite that is within
thy gates: and thou shalt rejoyce before the Lord thy God in all that
thou puttest thy haud unto. (As if he had said); when thou shalt re¬

0112.head: Chip.27. An Expofition upon tbe Book ot JOR. Vers.1e.

body.t: joys in all tbat thou puttest tby bands unto; be sure that thy re¬
joycing be before the Lord; chat is, in a sence of the presence of
the Lord with thee, who hath blessed thee, and caused thee to pro¬
sper in all that thou hast put thy hand unto. Thus Paul enjoynes
the Philippians (Phil. 3.1.) Fiually, my brethren, rejoyce in the
Lord: and (Chap. 4.4.) rejoyce in the Lord alway; and againe,
say rejoyce. This joy or delight in the Lord belongs to the first
Commandement; and therefore it is called natural worship, (not
naturall, as naturall is opposed to spiritual, but as naturall is oppo¬
sed to formal or instituted worship) because this delight is a wor¬
ship which we were to give unto God, confidered in himselfe,
though he had sot given any direction about it, as he hath done
about his externall worship. We kuow not in what particular
forme God will be worshipped, till he declares his own willi¬
bout it; and though we ought alwayes to be willing to worship
God, yet we must not give him a will-worship. But if we know
no more of God, chan that he is, we may know that we ought to
worship him by delighting in him, for that is a natural sequel
from the knowledg of him. And so to feare God, to trust upon
him, to belee ve in him, are acts of worship, which thevery disco¬
veries of God call us unto, though God had ucver published a law
requiring any such worship. But how little of this pure spirituall
worship hath God in the world ? how few are there that deliobt
God? Some caunot take any delight at all, if there be buta
mention of God; to discourse of God, puts them into a fit of Me¬
lancholly; they must put God out of the company, before they
can be merry or rejoyce, They lile not to retaine Gol in their kκoπ¬
ledge, (asthe Apostle speakes of the old Gentiles, Rom. 1. 28.)
and therefore the knouledg of God cannot at all be delightfull
them. Yes, how little of this internall and most spirituall wor¬
ship hath God from his own people? how little are they in think¬
ing and speaking of him with delight? How seldome are they
Ionging to enjoy him? how seldome rejoycing in the enjoymeut
of him?̀ though every one, who is truly godly doth truly delight
in God; yet it is to be charged upon most godly men, that they
are not filled with those delights. Tis rare to find Davids spirit,
who could say (Psal. 63.1.) O God, thou art my God, early vill
seek thet, my soul thirsteth for thet, my flesh longeth for thee, to
see thy pomer and thy glory, so as I'have seen it in the Sanctuary.

0113.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon tbe Bok ef Jo».

body.t: Vers.io.
They who have seen and tasted how gracious the Lord is, will be
calling for more luch sights and casts, and the more they have had
ot those sights and tasts, the more they will desire them. What
David had seen of God in the Sanctuary, he could not but desire
see igaine. And how doth he promise himself all delightful
satisfaction in God, could he but feed upon him in his thoughts,
(v.4, 5. of the same Plalme) My soul shall be satisfied mith mar¬
row and fatnesse, and my mouth shall praise thet with joyful lips;
when I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night
watches. As it is the property of a godly man to delight in God,
he doth promise, yea assure himself of more delights in God,
could he but get and keep his heart more to the meditation of
God.
Secondly, Observe;
A hypocrite doth not, will not, cannot truly deligbt in God.
He doth not, because he is carnal, and filled with the wisdome
of the flesh, and so with desires after and delights in fleshly things.
And until this fleshly mind, with which he is vainly pust up, and
which(in the very wisdome of it )is enmity against God, he neither
will nor can delight in God. The Lord saith ot the hypocritical
Jewes (Isa. 58. 2.) They seck me daily, and delight to knom my
wayts, as a Nation that did righteousnesse, &c. A hypocrite may
imitate those who delight in God and his wayes, but he hath no
real delight in either. The delight which he hath in worldly
things is seldome, if at all, hearty; for (as Solomon speaks, Prov.
14.13.) In laughter bis heart is sorromful, and the end of such
mirth is heaviness. As there is a worm at the root of his plea¬
sant gourd, which kills it, and causeth it to wither: so there is
worme, a gnawing worm at his heart oftentimes, which makes his
pleasures wither, while his gourd is green and flourishing. And
surely if the hypocrites delight in the best ot his temporal enjoy¬
ments be scarcely hearty, how heartlesse is his delight in spiritu¬
als? Till the affections are made spiritual there is no affection
to things that are spiritual. So then at best, the hypocrite who
takes but a poor delight in any thing, takes only a hypocritical
delight in the best things ot God, and in God who is best of all.
For, First, he hath no hope in God, therefore no delight in
God. He that is without hope, ie without God, and how can he

0114.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bok of JOB. Vers.1o.

body.t: havt delight in God who is without God.! The hypocrite is with¬
out any true hope at any time, and many times he is without so
much as a shew or shadow of hope. His hope (like his goodness)
is as a morning cloud, and as the early dew it goeth away. And if
the hope deferred maketh the heart sick, surely when hope in
God is quite departed and gone, the heart cannot delight in God,
There is no condition doth so much estrange the heart from God,
as a hopeless coudition (Jer. 18.12.) And they said, there is no
hope, (what will they do then? even run as farre from God as
they can? so it follows in the same place) But me will malk after
our onn devices, and we will every ont dot thi imagination of his
cvill heart.
Secondly, The hypocrite hath no suitablenesse in his heart to
God, therefore no delight in God. There must be some likenesse
between the faculty and the object, else there can be no delight
any kind whatsoever. Now what likenesse is there between
light and darknesse, between good and evill,between a holy God
and an unholy heart, between the true, the faithful God, and
false-hearted hypocrite?
Thirdly, The hypocrites delight is so carryed out to other
things, the streames of it are divided into so many channels, that
he hath none to spare for God; his delight runs to riches, to gold
and silver; his delight runs to pleasure, to the fat and sweet ot
the creature; his delight runs to honour, to dignities and prefer¬
ments among men; he delights in friends, yea he delights in sin
and wickednesse. All these sterle away his delight from God;
and put his mouth out of tast as to tasting that the Lord is graci¬
ous, or how gracious the Lord is. As Christ expostulates the mat¬
ter sharply & chidingly with the hypocritical Tewes, (Job.5.44.)
How can ye beleeve, wbich receive honour one of another, and setke
not the honour that cometh from God only? So we may expostulate
with the whole kind of hypocrites, How can ye delight in the Al¬
mighty, who take up your delights in the ereature, and seck not,
nor are at all satisfied with those delights that are in and come
from God only. If me delight not in God only, ve delight not in
Gol at all. As we cannot serve, so we cannot delight in God and
Mammon; for if we love the one, we uill hate the other, and
we delight in the one, we shall despise the other. As God de¬
spiseththose who delight in the creature, so they who delight in

0115.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Boik ef J0R. Verf.10,

body.t: the creature, will despise God; And if such say they do not, yet
God knows they do despise him, and doth interpret all fuch
pleasure taken in the creature,a contempt of himself. And hence
Christ denounceth, Noe unto them that laugh now, (Luke 6.25.)
That is, who laugh and rejoyce in worldly enjoyments, because
such joy and laughter is inconsistent with joy in God. The crei¬
ture may be the (medium or ) means of our delight, but God
only must be the object of it, or our delight may passe through
the creature, but it must determine in God alone.
Againe, Compare the former verse, (will God bear his cry,
mhen trouble cometh upon bim,) with this, will he alwayes delighi
himself in the Almighty?
Observe;
Unlesse the hypocrite get mhat he asks of God, he tabes no delight
in God,
The Psalmist calls all the prayers of hypocritical persons, flat¬
teries (Psal. 78.36.) When he slem them tbey sought bim, and
they returned aud enquired early after God, and they remembred
that God mas their rocke, and the high Gol their Redeemer, (that is,
they told God in prayer that he was their rock, ec.) Neverthi¬
lesse, they did but flatter bim mitb their moutb, and they lyed un¬
to bim mith their tongue, for their heart was xot rigbt mith him, That
is, they had no true love to, nor delight in God, only they would
faine have got help from him, and deliverance from their trou¬
bles. A flatterer doth not delight in the person flattered, but in
that which he hopes to obtain of him by flattery. And as their
hypocrisie did break out in their departures and backslidings from
God, as soon as they were essed of their fears, so the hypocrisie
of others, breaks out in their depa ture srom God, when they
cannot get their desires. The heart of a sincere man is of ano¬
ther frame and temper; for though God delay, yei deny him
an answer in that he prayeth foi, yet he de lighteth in him. He cry¬
eth to the Lord in sickuesse, in poverty, in straits, and the Lord
somtimes lets him lye sick, and poor, and straitned, and gives
him no reliefe; yet he delights and comforts hi self in God,
yez, God is better to him than thar he asks* the hand of God,
and therefore he takes pleasure in communion with God, though
God be not pleised to mend his condition. We may well suppofe

0116.head: Chap.27. An Expositon apon the Boit of JOR. Vers.1o.

body.t: that the Prophet Habbakuk prayed hard for the keeping off that
sore judgment of famine, yet in case famine should devour all,
and so his prayer not granted, yet his heart towards God was the
same, and his assurance strong, that his enjoyment of God alone,
would be as sweet to him, as in the greatest plenty of creature¬
enjoyments. (Hab. 3. 17.) Although the fig-tree shall not
blossome, neither shall fruit be in the Vines: the labour of the Olive
shall faile, and the fields shall yield no meate, the flock shall be cut off
from the fold, and there shall be no beard in the stalls; yet will I re¬
joyce in the Lord: I mill joy in the God of my salvation. A sincere
heart can feast in God, while he is starving in the creature; God is
good to him without the world as with it; and whatsoever
good he asks of God, God is better to him than what he asks,
except when he asks God himself. None pray purely to God,
but they who can rest satisfied with God, though God doth not
satisfie their desires in granting what they pray for,
Lastly, We may take these words, Will he delight himself in
the Almighty ? as a reason why the hypocrites cry is not heard;
God doth not hear his prayer, be cause he hath no delight in
God; he would have the mercies of God, but he cares not for
the God of his mercies, and so he hath neither.
Hence Observe;
E that doth not delight in Gol, is not heard of God.
The Lord can easily distinguish between a flatterer and anhum¬
ble petitioner. He kuows who come to him for his, or because
they kpow not what to do uithout him, and who come to him
for himielf, and because they love to be with him. (Psal. 37.4.)
Delight thy self als in the Lord, and be shall give thee the desires of
thint heart. As if David had said, Would you have the desires
of your heut given in, and your prayer granted, when you ask
of God, delighr your selves in God, and you have your desires.
This the Psalmist affirms, not only because God in whom the
soul delights, is more than all we can desire beside, but be¬
cause they who truly delight in God, are in the readiest way to
reccive all that they desire besides. Every man delights in the
things he heartily asks for; how glad would they be of riches,
who being poor, ask for riches? How glad would they be ot
health, who being sick, pray for health, &c.? But every godly

0117.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Vars.10.

body.t: man delights more in God of whom he asks, than in that, which
he asks of God; And therefore, as God gives himself, so that
which he desires too. It is the delight of God to hear those that
delight in him; And though Gods delighting inus is indeed the
cause of his granting our desires, yet it is our duty as weil as our
interest to delight in God, that we may have our desires granted.
When God sees that we rejoyce more in this, that he is our God,
than in all things else that can be given us, then he is ready to
give us all things else.The Lord was so well-pleased with Solomons
asking, when he asked a wise and an understanding heart to go¬
verne that great people, that the Lord gave him not only what
he asked, but what he asked not, riches and honour, (1 Kings3
11,12, 13.) Surely then, the Lord is so well-pleased with those
who ask and earnestly desire the enjoyment of himself, that he
cannot with-hold from them any lawful enjoyment, which is good
for them, and desired by them.
Now as the hypocrite, not delighting in God, is not heard
when he calls, so because he delighteth not in God, he will not
be long heard calling, as is shewed in the close of this verse.
will he alwayes call upon God?
The hypocrite prayeth, but he doth not hold out or persever
prayer. The Original words, which we translite alwayes, are
all time, that is, in all the due times and seasons of prayer; as
iTob had said, Will the hypocrite call upon God as often as the
providences of God and his own duty call him to pray ? They
pray almayes,'who pray when they ought, or as often and as long
as they ought. Thus the hypocrite will not alwayes call apon God;
He will not take his times and seasons to begin, nor will he con¬
tinue in it as he ought when he hath begun. We may be said to
do that alwayes, which we do as often as we are called, and
which we are alwayes ready and willing to doe, though not
called.
Hence note, first, from the Connection;
Unless me are in a frame to pray almayes, God will not heure us
at all,
That is, unless we would alwayes be in such a frame; The ho¬
liest man living may have his heart out of order, but he loves to

0118.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Vers.1o.

body.t: have it alwayes in order and ready for every good word and
worke. He would alwayes be in a praying frame: and he actuilly
prayeth in time of prosperity, as well as in time of adversity, in
time of peace, as well as in time of trouble, when all is well with
him, as well as when he is at the worst. Huless our spirit be
for prayer at all times, we make God our refuge only, not our
choyce, and are as they who would make use of a friend, but care
not at all to enjoy him. And will God hear such, when he sees
he should never hear of them, unlesse compelled to ask by ne¬
cessity. It is true, That God hears his people in many cases be¬
fore they cry, he prevents prayer, yet tis as true, God hears not
any, unlesse they pray alwayes, unlesse they pray continually.
And he that did ever pray (I do not say, he that ever said
prayer, or made a prayer, but he that did ever pray indeed) and
hath cryed Abba Father though but once, thorough the Spirit of
Adoptich, That man cannot but (in the sence explained ) be al¬
wayes praying.
Secondly, From the words considered in themselves, note;
It is our dut y to call upon God alwayes.
The text implies this clearly, other texts speak it plainly.
The Lord gives a Parable ( Luke 18.) and this is the scope of it,
(v. 1.) He spake a Parable unto them, to this end, that men ougbt
alwayes to pray, and not to faint. The Apostolical rules are, Pray
alwayes, mith all prayer and supplication in the spirit. (Eph.6.18.)
Pray without ceasing, (I Thess.5. 17.) There are many urgent
grounds why prayer must be continued.
First, We cannot subsist a minute without the assistance ot
God; for in him me live and move, and have our being, (Acts 17.
28.) And as we have our life, motion, and being, so the comforts
of our life, the guidance of our motions, and our well-being from
him. Therefore we must alwayes pray, both to acknowledge
our dependance, and to receive assistance from him.
Secondly, We are continually besieged with evils and temp¬
tations, we have enemies about us, either visible or invisible,
seen or unseen, therefore we have need to pray continually.
we had enemies alwayes in sight we would pray alwayes, we have
unseene enemies alwayes about us, and these are the most dange¬
rous enemies, therefore we hive more need alwayes to pray, and
Thirdly,
call in the aide ot God against them.

0119.head: Chap.27. An Exposition apon the Book of JOR. Vers.10.

body.t: Thirdly, We have work to do continually; if we know our
duty, we can never be out of work; and what-ever we do
we are to pray for help in it, and a blessing upon it. We rise
early in vain, and labour in vain, unlesse the Lord be with us in
all our labours.
Fourthly, We are continually using the creature, we use
food and rayment for the supply and support of our earthly Ta¬
bernacle; therefore we must pray continually. What good can
the creature do us without God? our bread cannot nourist us,
nor our cleiths keep us warme, but by a command from him.
As every creature of God is good (init self) so it is sanctified (unto
us) by the word ef God and prayer (1 Tim. 4.4,5.)
Fifthly, We are often in troubles and afflictions. Now the
rule is, Is any one afflicted, let him pray (James 5. 13. ) and if we
must pray as often as we are afflicted, we shall have cause to be
very often praying.
Sixthly, When we are at ease and quiet, in health and peace,
when the rock powrs us out rivers of oyl, and we wach our
footsteps (as once Tob did )with butter, even then we have need to
pray that our prosperity hurt us not, that we lose noc God in the
crowd of creature-comforts, thit we kick not against him (is Te¬
surun once did) while he makes us fat and flourishing.
Seventhly, We sin continually, we sin (is I may say) with¬
out ceasing, often doing that which is sinful, and sin alwayes
mingling it selfe with that we do; and therefore we had need to
pray continually, to mingle prayer with all we do, both for the
pardon of sin, or of what we do sinfully, as alio for power and
grace that we may do so nomore.
Eighthly, We ought continually to glorifie God, therefore
to pray continually; for though God may have glory by anyof
our actions or duties, yet the duty of prayer is that which gives
him the greatest glory, while we therein acknowledg his Allsuffi¬
ciency to do what we ask, and his goodnesse in being alwayes
ready to do it.
Yet this poynt is not so to be understood, as if we should doe
nothing else but pray, as some have ignorantly and erroneoufly
inferr’d from this, or such like Scriptures; for every man hath or
ought to have a calling in this world, wherein as the Apostle
speaks (1Cor. 7. 24.) He may abide mith God; That is, beth

0120.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Book of JOR. Verf.10,

body.t: with the good leave and favour of God, as also in a constant
communion with God, while he walkes according to the rule
and in the duty of it. We must doe nothing without prayer, but
we may doe many things besides praying.
Thirdly, Observe, ( which is implyed in the Question, will he
alwayes call upon God?)
A hypocrite will not alwayes call upon God,
You may see him set out very full of mettle; he sets out about
good duties, as some horses that will stand no ground in a mor¬
ning when they goe out, but they tire after an houres riding,
they will not travel all the day; so a hypocrite may set out with
great deale of mettle, but will he pray alwayes? no, he will be
weary of duty, and throw it up at last. And he throws it up upon
these, upon either of these two occasions; both which we may
take notice of from the text.
First, When he speeds not in prayer, then he will throw up
prayer; When he seeth nothing come, he cannot goe on; will he
continue when there is no answer? no appearance of an answer?
or when God seemes in his providence to speik contrary to his
prayer? will he now persevere in calling upon God? no; he hath
no desire to duty when he cannot get what he desires by duty.
It is with him as with some draft Horses, they will draw when the
load is coming, but if they feel it not coming, they trample and
will not draw: But take a horse of a right breed,and put his traces
toa tree or a post, he will straine and straine, and dye upon the
phce, though nothing come, before he will give it over; Thus ’tis
in this case; a godly man though he feele not the petition come
for which he asks, whether in spiritualls or temporals (it may be
he hath prayed many a yeare for such or such a mercy, and cannot
get it) yet he will pray still. He knows it is his duty to waite
well as to pray; and though the Lord let him waite long, yet he
will pray still, without limiting the holy one of Israel. It shewes
very gracious heart, to be encouraged by the experience we have
of the Lords answering prayer to pray still. But itis an argument
of a more gracious heart, not to be discouraged fromn continuing
in prayer, when we get no answer. This Spirit ot holy courag¬
never ledg’d in the heart of a hypocrite; if God will not doe waat
he prayeth for, he hath done praying.

0121.head: Chap.27. An Exposition upon the Bok ef JOR. Vers.10.

body.t: Secondly, Take the contrary; If the hypocrite speed in pray¬
er, and get what he askes, then also he thromes up prayer, and
will aske no more. If from a sick-bed he be raised to health, he
leaves prayer behind him (as it were) sick a bed; He growes
weak in calling upon God, when at his call, God hath given him
strength. And thus tis in any other instance. When he hath got
what he had a mind to in prayer, he hath no more mind toptay:
whereas a godly man prayes after he hath sped as he did before,
and though he fall not into those troubles againe, and so is not
occasioned to urge those petitions againe, which he did in trou¬
ble, yet he cannot live without prayer ; because he cannot live
out of communion with God. The creature is as the white of an
egge, tastlesse to him, unlesse he enjoy God. David saith (Pl.116.
1, 2.)I love the Lord, because he hath beard my voyce and my sup¬
plication; that is, because he hath granted me that which I sup¬
plicated to him for; but did this graut of what he had asked, take
him off from asking more? the next words shew us, what his re¬
solution was upon that grant; Because he batb enclined his ear
unto me, therefore I will call upon him as long as I live; as if he had
said, I will never give over praying, forasmuch as I have been
heard in prayer. It is reported of one who alwayes laid a nett
upon his table when he went to meat, to mind him of his duty,
fish for soules in his pastorall care and office (as was pretended
ot him, I say, it is reported) that when he had attained to high pre¬
ferment, he laid aside the use of his nett at table,and being asked
why, answered, that he had now got that which he had been fish¬
ing for. He had catch his fish, and therefore cared no more for
his nett. Thus the hypocrite puts away his nett of prayer, when
once he hath taken the fish, the benefit which he desired aud la¬
boured for. In both these cases we may put Tobs Question, will
the bypocrite pray alwajes? If he can get nothing, he saith, why
should I waite upon God any longer? What profit is it to pray
unto him? And if once he get his profit, he saith, what need I pray
any longer, I have what I would have; and then he either growes
remisse and slack in duty, or layes it quite aside. He never sought
God for himselfe, but himselfe in secking God; and so having
found what he desired for himselfe in seeking God, he hath no
desire, or but a very cold one, to seek God any more. There¬
sore

0122.head: Chap.27. Au Exposition upon the Bock of JOB. Vers.10.

body.t: Lastly, Comparing the two parts of the text (will he delight
bimself in the Almighty, mill he alwayes call upon God? I say, com¬
paring these) together, we may for conclusion of this verse,
Observe;
They that delight in God (and they only) will alwayes call
upon God, or persevere to the end in prayer.
The reason is, because God is the same alwayes without any
variablenesse or shadow of turning. A sincere beleever sees he
hath as much need of God, when he hath supplye d all his present
needs, as he had before. And he kuows God is as good, as gra¬
cious, as desireable as ever he was, though he delay or deny the
grant of that which he hath desired; so that whatsoever God dis¬
penceth or giveth out to him, whether good or evill, bitter or
sweet, dark or light, griefe or sorrow, he still keeps close to
God, and will alwayes be making his addresses and applications at
the throne of Gsace. God is sweeter to him than all the mer¬
cies and blessings, than all the graces and comforts which he hath
given him; and God is exceeding sweet to him, though he doth
not presently give him the mercies, aud the blessings, the exercise
of those graces, and the feeling of those comforts which he hath
prayed for.
To close all, We have three things remarkable in these two
verses concerning the hypocrite. First, The Hypocrite delights not
God; There's his sin. Secondly, God hears not the cry of the by¬
pocrite; That’s his misery. Thirdly, The hypocrite mill not almayes
call upon God, That’s both his sip, and his misery. It is a great sin
not to call uvon God, and none are more miserable than thay
who doe not callpon him; for their misery is irremovable.
From all, Tobs infe-s, that he was no hypocrite; for though God
did not presently heare him so as to deliver him, yet he delighted
the Almighty, and would continue praying to him, and trusting
upon him, though he should slay him.

Behold, all ye your selves have seen it, mhy then are ye

-He two former verses of this Context are a preface, wherein
A Tob persuadeth his friends to hearken to what he should fur¬

First, That though he had all along denyed himselse to be

Secondly, That though Gods proceedings with wicked men

Verse 11. I mill teach you by the hand of Gol.
The word which we render to teach, hath a three-fold signifi¬
cation in Scripture.
First, Properly it signifies to cast, or throw a thing cut of the
haud, to throm a dart or a stone, and to cast a lot.
Secondly, It signifies to raine; and the reason of it is, because
rain is cast cut of the clouds, and (as it were) shot down from
heaven upon the Earth, to moisten and make it fruitfull.
Thirdlv, By a mecapbor, and in allusion to both the former,
the word sigr.sies (as ue translate it here) to teach: Right teach¬
ing, is a testinger darting of lessons and mbolesome truths into the
mind. It is allo a raining, a distilling, a droping of instructions
uto the understauding, from whence ther soale into the mill and af¬

0124.head: Chap.27. An Expositon npon the Boik of JOR. Vers.11.

body.t: fections; and so those who receive them are made fruit full in practice,
When Moses was about to make his last or dying Sermon toIs¬
rael, he insists much upon this metaphor, My doctrine shall drop

2.)And in the 34th Chapter of this booke, Eliha preferring the

but in the teaching of God. The Hebrew is, mho raineth like him?
No man ever powred out such raines or distilled such dews of ho¬
Iy doctrine as God doth; He with a word can make that heart
and the life which before was a dry heath or barren wilderness,
bud or blossom like Eden, to spring like a watered garden.
But though it be true which Elibu said, that no man can teach
or raine down like God, yet man must venture and doe his part,
He may say to his Brother or friend, as Job here did, I will teach
Cor drop doctrine upon) you by the hand of God.
Hence Note;
It is a duty to teach those who are ignorant and out of the way.
It is a duty to learn, but it is a higher duty to teach; it is good
to receive Instruction, but it is better to give it. David having
prayed earnestly that God would give him a new experience of
his free grace in the pardon of his sin, promiseth (Psal. 51.13.)
Then mill I teach transgressors thy nayes, and sinners shall be con¬

(Luk. 22.32.) When thou art converted strengthen thy brethren;
strengthen them by instruction, and strengthen them with conso¬

body.t: of sin, and the grace of God in themselves to beale their sinfullness.
I mill teach you by the hand of God.
There are considerable differences in the reading of this clause.
First, Some thus; I teach you being ander the hand of Gol;
As if he had said, I being nom sorely corrected and chastened by the

afflictions are Instructions; and they who have been long af¬
fflicted, are best able to give instruction, especially in the dealings
of God with the afflicted : none have spoken such lessons, prea¬
ched such Sermons, as they who have been under the hand ot
God. Chastisings make men wise, and spiritually learned, able to
teach indeed. I ( saith Tob) being under the hand of God will teach
you, and because you see me under the hand of God, you may be
sure that I will teach you nothing but the truth, and in the truth
or sincerity of my heart. “Tis no time to speak flatteries aud
falsehoods; I am ready to dye, and I will speak my mind ( and

man should speake none but words of weight, and his words
should have weight with all the living.
Secondly, The text is rendred thus, I mill teach you of the hand

done. Your opinion is, that God bestowes outward good things

0126.head: Chap. 27. An Exposition upon tbe Boœk of J0B. Verf.11.

body.t: But the truth is, outward good or evill, fall indifferently from the
hand of God upon the good and upon the evill, as to himselse

those acts and administrations of God which are done by his hand

them what is in the hand or power of God, as all the afflictions
and comforts of the children of men are. This reading containes
also a cleare truth, and a very usefull one; How can our tongues
be better imployed than in teaching what the hand ot God hath
done, or what the workes of God are both in creation and provi¬
dence. God speakes much to us by his hand, and we ought to be
continually speaking of the hand of God ; yet I conceive this text
doth not clearly lead us to that doctrine, and therefore I shall not
stay uponit.
Thirdly, We translite;
I will teach you by the band of God
And so the meaning of it is, first, I will teach you bythe helpe

body.t: Hence Observe;
All tbings are mith and before God.
They are alwayes in his Councels, he hath an idea ot what is

ui. -

Secondly, Thus; They shall be buried in death; that is, they
shall be forgotten as soon as they dye; to be so, is a Judgment.
Then a man is properly & iudeed buried in death, when he is for¬
gotten as soone as he is dead, and no sooner out of the world, but
out of all mens minds, unlesse to think and speak of him with
abhorrence. Thus to say a man is buried in death, is as much as
say, he shall not be remembred with credit when he is dead.
Some are thus buried in life or alive, and many are thus buried in
death. This is a faire interpretation.

The pestilence is a very greivous and sore judgment, 'tis death.

But though we have no cause to wonder, yet we have much
cause to lament, while we see the sons of men thus busied in the
carth, and in love with earthly things. How sad is it to see so ma¬
ny venture the perishing of their mortal bodies, much more ot
their immortal souls, in sceking thinge vehich perish? Hou sad
to see their hunger after this prey, carrying them into pathi
which the Lyons thelp sever trod, aor the fierce Lyon ever pas¬
sed? How sad is it to see such digging and searching for silver and
gold, while that is neglected chich is better then gold, even dera¬
ble substauce? Hou sad is ic to sce men overcoming all difficul¬
ties and laughing at all dangers to get gold, uhen as every diffi¬
culty stops their search aster heavenly treasures. It a siaad (hall
say) breat out upon tbem, nay, if but a few drops ot trouble fall
upon them, they have done presently; and, if a rock, & a moun¬
tain (shall I say) be in the way, nay, it but a petble stons er mole¬
bill of opposition be in theit uay, they will goe no further; O how
sar are they from cutting rocks, or labouring to remove moun¬
tains! How sad is it to see men slighting the shadow of death in
their search for gold, and yet affraid of deaths shadou, even the
remotest appearance of death in their searches after God? what
shame is it to see men pass not ouly through the shadow of death,
but through death indeed, fot dying or rather lifelest things,
and yet to be affraid ot deatbs shadow, in following the things ot
eternal life! When the fluggard should goe on in his way, he vill
not, for (saith he (Pro. 26. 13. )There is a Lyon in the way; eve¬
ry shew of danger is to him a Lyon, though possibly it can endan¬
ger him no more then a mouse. What a shame and reproich is it
to mankinde, that whereas in seeking gold and silver, men have
exceeded all the fabulous labours ot the old gunts, by their real
labours, that yet men in secking grace and glory, a& so much be¬
low even duarfs and pigmyes?
Be exhorted therefore, not to think any paines too much, or
perils too great for the things of heaven, secing men think no
paines too much, nor perils perilous for the things of the earth.
The very labour in secking heavenly treasure is very sweet, but
the enjoyment of them is infinitely sweeter: uhereas the labour of
secking for earthly treasures, is very tirefome, and the very enjoy¬

There is nothing can divert the thoughts of man and his de¬

of God are more then a diversion of our thoughts from the world,
they are the death and mortification ot them. Earthly desires can¬
not live in the aire of heaven, no more then any creature can,
when taken out of or off trom its proper element. The gladness
nhich the light of Gods countenance puts into the heart, con¬

puts into the heart. As God alone will be All in all to Saints in
heaven, so they who are much vith him here in the actings ot faith
and love, cannot but delight in him above all, and rise up to Da¬
vids conclusion, from Davids Questions (Psal. 73. 25.) Rhom

Thus far Job hath described the labour ot man, in seeking

course he comes to shew that there is a vein of wisdom, which
few men in the world have a desire to seck, and which none of
the men of the world have an ability find.

N the former part of this Chapter, we found Job discoursing ot
that natural wisdom which is implanted in man by God.
And there he shews by an induction of many instances, what
that wisdom can doe, how far it can work; that, can search the
bosome and bowels of the earth, and discern uhat’s there; that
can fetch or draw out gold and silver and precious stones from
thence; that can master and overcome all the difficulties aud im¬
pediments, and out dare all the dangers that stand in the way ot
those attainments; that wisdom can purifie and refine, perfect
and polish all sorts of metals and gemms, into a fituess for the
use and ornament of man : all this the wisdom of man can doe.
Most men can see far into nature; some men can see her quite
through, they are (as it were) of councel with nature, and
know her whole heart, all her secrets: allthis man doth and hath
by natural wisdom, which yet is the gift of God to man, A gift
common to man as man. So that there is nothing in this lower
world, nothing in the lowest parts of this world, which-hath nct

But now (in the following part of this Chapter, as was toucht

those works of God in providence which are done aloft upon the
face of the earth.
Vers. 12. But whert suall wisdom be found?
Man, who hath digg’d and found out many secrets, knows not

First, Because there is no place particularly designed for it;

with much excellent variety. (Ver. 12, 13, 14.) ubere shall mis¬

Secondly, Because man hath no price in his hand to obtain it;
As these is no place in nature where it can be found, so all the

not compassable by (that price for which the old heathens faid

Gold and Silver are the most valuable things in this world.
VVhat cannot Cold and Silver buy? yea, what cannot Gold and

said, All things are to be sold or saleable at Roms. Gold may get
any thing of them who are covetous of Gold. Not only Dignities
and Offices, but indulgences and pardons, Altars and Crosses, the
power of the keys, and Christ himself, with Heaven and all, are
set to fale in open market by those Romish Merchants. But the
things which are highly esteemed among men are an abomination
to the Lord.
Further, The word here rendred Gold,signifies, shut up or en¬
closed; Gold is so cilled upona double consideration.
First, VVith respect to the natural locality of Gold; For as
some Gold is mingled uith the sand, and lies open to the eye up-

of the earth, or shut in among stones and rocks. This enclo¬
sed Gold is the best and richest Gold; and yet for this, wisdom
cannot be gotten.

of ingratitude not to bless men when we receive any good from

to bless Jesus Christ, who hath at once procured us thie greatest

heart; because as true joy springs from the heart, so that’s true
which is hearty; possibly there may be a song in the mouth, when

in, there': cause of joy without, though there be no outuard
joycing.
VVhen Job saith, I caused the vidous heart to sing for joy,
this notes a wondersul change in the widows state; the wid¬

dous heart to sing ? First, he desiuered her from her enemies;
secondly, he releived her in her necessities; either of these two
uayes the vidows heart is caused to sing for joy.
